From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Hugo_1989-09-21_1900Z.png/250px-Hugo_1989-09-21_1900Z.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hugo_1989-09-21_1900Z.png)

[Hurricane Hugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hugo "Hurricane Hugo") approaching South Carolina as a Category 4 hurricane on September 21, 1989

Since 1851, 132 [tropical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone "Tropical cyclone") or [subtropical cyclones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_cyclone "Subtropical cyclone") have either directly or indirectly affected the state of [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"), with the most recent being [Chantal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Chantal_(2025) "Tropical Storm Chantal (2025)") in [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2025 Atlantic hurricane season").

## List of storms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: List of storms")]

### Pre–1900

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Pre–1900")]

*   August 24–25, 1851 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1851_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Four "1851 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   August 28, 1852 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1852_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_One "1852 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   October 10, 1852 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1852_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Five "1852 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   September 9, 1854 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1854_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Three "1854 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   September 1, 1856 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1856_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Five "1856 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   September 17, 1859 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1859_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Five "1859 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through northwestern portions of the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   June 22, 1867 – A Category 1 [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1867_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_One "1867 Atlantic hurricane season") made landfall to the east of [Charleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_South_Carolina "Charleston, South Carolina").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   August 28, 1871 – A [tropical depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1871_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Four "1871 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through southern portions of the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   October 6, 1871 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1871_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Seven "1871 Atlantic hurricane season") moved southern portions of the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   September 20, 1873 – A fast-moving [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1873_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Three "1873 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through southern portions of the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   September 28, 1874 – A Category 1 [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1874_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Six "1874 Atlantic hurricane season") made landfall near [Seabrook Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seabrook_Island,_South_Carolina "Seabrook Island, South Carolina").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   October 4, 1877 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1877_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Four "1877 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   September 12, 1878 – A Category 1 [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1878_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Five "1878 Atlantic hurricane season") made landfall near [Edisto Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edisto_Beach,_South_Carolina "Edisto Beach, South Carolina").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   September 11, 1882 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1882_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Two "1882 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through northwestern portions of the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   September 11–12, 1884 – A slow-moving [tropical depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1884_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Three "1884 Atlantic hurricane season") struck the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   August 25, 1885 – A Category 2 [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1885_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Two "1885 Atlantic hurricane season") made landfall on [Kiawah Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiawah_Island "Kiawah Island"). 21 deaths were reported.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-deadliest-4)
*   October 12, 1885 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1885_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Tropical_Storm_Eight "1885 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   June 22, 1886 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1886_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Two "1886 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   July 1, 1886 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1886_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Three "1886 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   October 20, 1887 – A [tropical depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1887_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Thirteen "1887 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   September 10, 1888 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1888_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Tropical_Storm_Five "1888 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   September 24, 1889 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1889_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Six "1889 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   June 16, 1893 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1893_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_One "1893 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   August 27, 1893 – The devastating [Sea Islands Hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Islands_Hurricane "Sea Islands Hurricane") struck the [Sea Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Islands "Sea Islands") region of Georgia and South Carolina, causing major damage. An estimated 1,000–2,000 people were killed between both states.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-deadliest-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-5)
*   October 4, 1893 – A [tropical storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1893_Cheni%C3%A8re_Caminada_hurricane "1893 Chenière Caminada hurricane") moved through the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   October 13, 1893 – A Category 3 [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1893_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Nine "1893 Atlantic hurricane season") made landfall near [McClellanville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McClellanville,_South_Carolina "McClellanville, South Carolina"), causing major damage. 15 deaths were reported.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   September 27, 1894 – A Category 1 [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1894_Greater_Antilles_hurricane "1894 Greater Antilles hurricane") made landfall near [Port Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Royal,_South_Carolina "Port Royal, South Carolina").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   October 10, 1894 – After impacting Georgia, a [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1894_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Five "1894 Atlantic hurricane season") entered southwestern South Carolina briefly as a Category 1, later impacting other portions of the state as a tropical storm.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   July 8, 1896 – A [tropical depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1896_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_One "1896 Atlantic hurricane season") moved through northwestern parts of the state.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   September 29, 1896 – The [Cedar Key hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1896_Cedar_Key_hurricane "1896 Cedar Key hurricane") moved through South Carolina as a Category 2 hurricane, producing significant damage. Seven deaths were reported.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   August 31, 1898 – A Category 1 [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1898_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Two "1898 Atlantic hurricane season") made landfall near [Hilton Head Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilton_Head_Island,_South_Carolina "Hilton Head Island, South Carolina").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)
*   October 31, 1899 – A Category 2 [hurricane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1899_Atlantic_hurricane_season#Hurricane_Nine "1899 Atlantic hurricane season") made landfall near [Myrtle Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myrtle_Beach,_South_Carolina "Myrtle Beach, South Carolina").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-NOAA-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-u.s._hurricanes-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_South_Carolina_hurricanes#cite_note-HURDAT-3)

### 1900–1949

*   September 29–30, 1959 – [Hurricane Gracie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Gracie "Hurricane Gracie") made landfall near [Edisto Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edisto_Island,_South_Carolina "Edisto Island, South Carolina") as a Category 4 hurricane with sustained winds of 130 mph (215 km/h) on September 29, causing major damage. Water levels of 8.14 feet (2.48 m) were observed in [Charleston Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston_Harbor "Charleston Harbor"), while wind gusts estimated near 150 mph (240 km/h) occurred in coastal [Beaufort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaufort_County,_South_Carolina "Beaufort County, South Carolina"), [Colleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colleton_County,_South_Carolina "Colleton County, South Carolina") and [Charleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston_County,_South_Carolina "Charleston County, South Carolina") counties. [Hurricane Hugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hugo "Hurricane Hugo") approaching South Carolina as a Category 4 hurricane on September 21, 1989

Since 1851, 132 [tropical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone "Tropical cyclone") or [subtropical cyclones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_cyclone "Subtropical cyclone") have either directly or indirectly affected the state of [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"), with the most recent being [Chantal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Chantal_(2025) "Tropical Storm Chantal (2025)") in [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2025 Atlantic hurricane season").

## Selecting Storms

×

### Getting Storm Details

Storms can be selected by clicking a row in the table or a track in the map, which will highlight the storm track on the map. For more detailed track and summary information about the selected storm, click the Get Storm Details button.

### Filtering Storms

The Filter Storms button opens up options for filtering storms by year, storm category, and others. Applying the filters will limit the display of storms in the map and table.

### Searching the Table

Storms can be searched by name, year, or any keywords found in the table. For example, typing "flood" in the search box will return all storms that have "flood" somewhere in the description. This option does not filter the map.

### Table View

Storm data can be viewed in a table-only web page, along with storms prior to 1851, in the [Table View.](https://www.dnr.sc.gov/climate/sco/hurricanes/table-view.html) The Table View is less interactive and may be easier to navigate for some users.

# How many more hurricanes will hit Myrtle Beach? Here are fall 2023 weather predictions.

 By [Eleanor Nash](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/profile/269540007/)

Updated September 10, 2023 1:29 PM[![Image 5: Gift Icon](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/zlisob-yon/data/giftArticle/giftIcon.png)Gift Article](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/news/weather-news/article279168489.html)

![Image 6: Rain bands passed over downtown Myrtle Beach on Wednesday, Aug. 30 as Tropical Storm Idalia approached the Grand Strand.](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/public/latest-news/jiaxcn/picture278799539/alternates/LANDSCAPE_1200/D86A8747.jpg)

 Rain bands passed over downtown Myrtle Beach on Wednesday, Aug. 30 as Tropical Storm Idalia approached the Grand Strand.  Jason Lee JLee@thesunnews.com

Autumn in the Myrtle Beach area means enjoying cooler weather and watching hurricane forecasts. But how much cooler will temperatures be this year? And how many hurricanes are coming to the Grand Strand?

While we won’t know specifics until the weather arrives, the National Weather Service in Wilmington released its [fall 2023 climate outlook](https://www.weather.gov/ilm/FallOutlook2023), sharing long-term predictions for September, October and November. Here is what we know about the fall weather, from the NWS.

### How many more hurricanes are coming?

In 2023, Myrtle Beach has experienced one tropical storm so far – Idalia, [which dropped](https://twitter.com/NWSWilmingtonNC/status/1697248938527764535) up to 7.4 inches of rain on Horry County. Currently, Hurricane Lee is [passing north](https://www.facebook.com/NWSNHC/posts/pfbid02BuenwQbMTuC9vwMfrLForrUZV1MVVSTJMeqKRa5Ya3yBKVB5FTqjCo9UL9RQ1SDEl) of the Caribbean Islands, and is expected to bring rip currents and dangerous surf conditions to the Myrtle Beach area this week.

September is the most active month for tropical storms in the Myrtle Beach area, with 40% of all storms and hurricanes since 1870 hitting during that month.

This year, four hurricanes have formed in the Atlantic Basin, compared to NOAA’s [predicted 6-11 hurricanes](https://www.thestate.com/news/state/south-carolina/article278164432.html) from June through November. NOAA expected two to five of these major hurricanes to form in 2023, and so far, Idalia and Lee have both developed winds of 111 mph or greater.

### Will we have a hot or wet fall?

After a summer with normal temperatures and amounts of rain, the Climate Prediction Center [expects](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/predictions/long_range/seasonal.php?lead=1) above average temperatures and precipitation in the Myrtle Beach area during fall.

However, the amount of rain the Grand Strand receives depends on the number and intensity of tropical storms, according to the NWS. The first frost usually occurs in mid-November in the Myrtle Beach area.

### What will water temperatures be this fall?

In Myrtle Beach, the water temperature typically stays in the 80s until mid-September and in the 70s through mid-October, according to NWS historical data.

If you get into the water, be careful of rip currents. Fall hurricanes can increase the risk of [rip currents](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/news/state/south-carolina/article276029656.html), even if these storms stay far away from shore. September was the month with the most strong and moderate rip current reports since 2004 in Wrightsville Beach, North Carolina.

This story was originally published September 10, 2023 at 1:09 PM.

# How many more hurricanes will hit Myrtle Beach? Here are fall 2023 weather predictions.

 By [Eleanor Nash](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/profile/269540007/)

Updated September 10, 2023 1:29 PM[![Image 5: Gift Icon](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/zlisob-yon/data/giftArticle/giftIcon.png)Gift Article](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/news/weather-news/article279168489.html)

![Image 6: Rain bands passed over downtown Myrtle Beach on Wednesday, Aug. 30 as Tropical Storm Idalia approached the Grand Strand.](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/public/latest-news/jiaxcn/picture278799539/alternates/LANDSCAPE_1200/D86A8747.jpg)

 Rain bands passed over downtown Myrtle Beach on Wednesday, Aug. 30 as Tropical Storm Idalia approached the Grand Strand.  Jason Lee JLee@thesunnews.com

Autumn in the Myrtle Beach area means enjoying cooler weather and watching hurricane forecasts. But how much cooler will temperatures be this year? And how many hurricanes are coming to the Grand Strand?

While we won’t know specifics until the weather arrives, the National Weather Service in Wilmington released its [fall 2023 climate outlook](https://www.weather.gov/ilm/FallOutlook2023), sharing long-term predictions for September, October and November. Here is what we know about the fall weather, from the NWS.

### How many more hurricanes are coming?

In 2023, Myrtle Beach has experienced one tropical storm so far – Idalia, [which dropped](https://twitter.com/NWSWilmingtonNC/status/1697248938527764535) up to 7.4 inches of rain on Horry County. Currently, Hurricane Lee is [passing north](https://www.facebook.com/NWSNHC/posts/pfbid02BuenwQbMTuC9vwMfrLForrUZV1MVVSTJMeqKRa5Ya3yBKVB5FTqjCo9UL9RQ1SDEl) of the Caribbean Islands, and is expected to bring rip currents and dangerous surf conditions to the Myrtle Beach area this week.

September is the most active month for tropical storms in the Myrtle Beach area, with 40% of all storms and hurricanes since 1870 hitting during that month.

This year, four hurricanes have formed in the Atlantic Basin, compared to NOAA’s [predicted 6-11 hurricanes](https://www.thestate.com/news/state/south-carolina/article278164432.html) from June through November. NOAA expected two to five of these major hurricanes to form in 2023, and so far, Idalia and Lee have both developed winds of 111 mph or greater.

### Will we have a hot or wet fall?

After a summer with normal temperatures and amounts of rain, the Climate Prediction Center [expects](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/predictions/long_range/seasonal.php?lead=1) above average temperatures and precipitation in the Myrtle Beach area during fall.

However, the amount of rain the Grand Strand receives depends on the number and intensity of tropical storms, according to the NWS. The first frost usually occurs in mid-November in the Myrtle Beach area.

### What will water temperatures be this fall?

In Myrtle Beach, the water temperature typically stays in the 80s until mid-September and in the 70s through mid-October, according to NWS historical data.

If you get into the water, be careful of rip currents. Fall hurricanes can increase the risk of [rip currents](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/news/state/south-carolina/article276029656.html), even if these storms stay far away from shore. September was the month with the most strong and moderate rip current reports since 2004 in Wrightsville Beach, North Carolina.

This story was originally published September 10, 2023 at 1:09 PM.

## **Overview**

A strengthening low pressure system in the eastern Gulf of America on December 16, 2023 moved northeast across Florida and along the Southeast U.S. coast December 17 and 18. Near hurricane-force wind gusts, significant rainfall and tidal flooding, and an EF-1 tornado occurred across portions of southeast NC,northeast SC and the adjacent Atlantic Ocean.
[![Image 3: GOES infrared satellite image of the major coastal storm of December 17-18, 2023](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/IRloop.gif)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/IRloop.gif)WPC Surface Analyses

Start Loop Stop Loop



![Image 4](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/loops/CoastalStormDec2023_WPC/SFCmap_121523_12Z_1.gif)![Image 5](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/loops/CoastalStormDec2023_WPC/SFCmap_121523_12Z_1.gif)![Image 6](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/loops/CoastalStormDec2023_WPC/SFCmap_121623_00Z_2.gif)![Image 7](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/loops/CoastalStormDec2023_WPC/SFCmap_121623_12Z_3.gif)![Image 8](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/loops/CoastalStormDec2023_WPC/SFCmap_121723_00Z_4.gif)![Image 9](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/loops/CoastalStormDec2023_WPC/SFCmap_121723_12Z_5.gif)![Image 10](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/loops/CoastalStormDec2023_WPC/SFCmap_121823_00Z_6.gif)![Image 11](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/loops/CoastalStormDec2023_WPC/SFCmap_121823_12Z_7.gif)
The storm was a ["nor'easter"](https://www.weather.gov/safety/winter-noreaster) -- a non-tropical low pressure system that produces strong northeast winds along the coastline. While nor'easters are not uncommon during the fall, winter, and early spring, this was a particularly strong one with [record low sea level pressure readings for December](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/research/roth/DecemberRecordLowSLPs.gif)(see below).Unlike tropical systems (e.g., tropical storms and hurricanes), nor'easters feed off the temperature differences between cold and warm air masses, which is why they are most common during cooler months when the land can cool down a lot more than the Atlantic Ocean.

**Record Low Sea Level Pressures Set for December:**

* Wilmington, NC (ILM) - 985.4 mb (29.10 in Hg)

* N Myrtle Beach, SC (CRE) - 988.1 mb (29.18 in Hg)

* Myrtle Beach, SC (MYR) - 989.2 mb (29.21 in Hg)[![Image 12](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/WPCanal.jpg)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/WPCanal.jpg)

## **Rainfall**

A surface [trough](https://forecast.weather.gov/glossary.php?word=Trough) along the coast along with[deep moisture](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/pwat_121723_18Z.PNG)and strong [mid-level moisture transport](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/h85mtrans_121723_18Z.PNG)led to abundant[moisture convergence](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/mconv_121723_18Z.PNG)and very heavy rainfall across much of the area. The heaviest rainfall was focused along the SC coast and led to significant flash flooding, especially in [Georgetown](https://twitter.com/ReedTimmerAccu/status/1736546082627141720?s=20) and Horry Counties where widespread totals of 6+"were observed with locally higher amounts of 10-15". Daily rainfall records were even set for December 17 at all 4 of our official climate sites: N. Myrtle Beach, SC (CRE) - 3.59", Florence, SC (FLO) - 2.39", Wilmington, NC (ILM) - 3.23" and Lumberton, NC (LBT) - 4.08".

[![Image 13: Wilmington, NC Doppler Radar (KLTX) precipitation estimate from 12 UTC December 16 to 12 UTC December 18, 2023](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/STA_121823.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/STA_121823.png)

**Wilmington, NC doppler radar (KLTX) dual pol 24-hr precipitation accumulation ending 1216 UTC (716 AM EST) on December 18, 2023.**

[![Image 14: Rainfall analysis from 12 UTC December 16 to 12 UTC December 18, 2023](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/CoastalStorm_Dec2023_Rainfall.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/CoastalStorm_Dec2023_Rainfall.png)

**48-hr precipitation analysis from 12 UTC (7 AM EST) December 16 to 12 UTC (7 AM EST) December 18, 2023 across southeast NC and northeast SC.**

## **Coastal Flooding**

The tidal forecast was definitely one of the most challenging aspects of this event. As is typical in such nor'easters, we anticipated a significant risk from coastal flooding but trying to pinpoint the exact water levels everywhere along the coast is always difficult, especially given the uncertainty regarding the storm's track/timing/strength. This is especially the case at our 3 Total Water Level (TWL) forecast sites - [Springmaid Pier in Myrtle Beach,SC](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/MROS1), [Johnnie Mercer's Pier in Wrightsville Beach, NC](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/JMPN7) and [along the Cape Fear River at Wilmington, NC](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/WLON7).

Persistent, strong north to northeast winds helped raise water levels along the coast prior to the storm's arrival from the south. Water levels then peaked during the afternoon on Sunday, December 17 around the time of the strongest onshore winds, although this was several hours after the highest astronomical tides. Thus, water levels could have been higher if the peak [storm surge](https://w1.weather.gov/glossary/index.php?word=storm+surge)occurred closer to high astronomical tide!The highest water level recorded at [Springmaid Pier](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/MROS1) was 9.97 ft above Mean Lower Low Water (MLLW) / 4.37 ft above Mean Higher High Water (MHHW), which was one of the highest tides on record at the time (and highest tide not related to a tropical cyclone!). At [Wilmington](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/WLON7), the tide peaked at 7.03 ft MLLW / 2.35 ft MHHW. However, the greatest surge occurred closer to low tide at [Wrightsville Beach](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/JMPN7) and thus, only minor coastal flooding levels were reached there. Ultimately, minor to moderate coastal flooding occurred across the area, with the greatest water levels south of Cape Fear, including [Pawleys Island, SC](https://twitter.com/PawleysIslandPD/status/1736432136419193085?s=20), [Myrtle Beach, SC](https://twitter.com/AndrewElswickWX/status/1736450832357261393?s=20), [N. Myrtle Beach, SC](https://twitter.com/accuweather/status/1736461314690896369?s=20),[Cherry Grove, SC](https://www.facebook.com/MeteorologistJamieArnold/posts/pfbid02yhUkYnFauGst5jeGfhMtqWCqpzgwhqHRm3dbKqVSW9x4DmGDW15FKsA64NJuZ1Gjl),[Ocean Isle Beach, NC](https://twitter.com/MaraMcJiltonTV/status/1736474115568017583?s=20)and [Southport, NC](https://www.facebook.com/brunswicksheriffNC/posts/pfbid02aHTSbRoJheZGjiHXdLkBSymyy6HN7hajZsy3my96EVBHVmEqZGTid4NrUz7LSgsWl).

## **Winds**

[Wind gusts](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=PNSILM&e=202312182051) reached tropical storm force (>=39 mph) across much of the region, a combination of pressure gradient winds and convective winds, as well as from a[gravity wave](https://w1.weather.gov/glossary/index.php?word=gravity%20wave)(around Florence, SC). The strong winds and heavy rainfall loosened up the soils and resulted in some downed trees/power lines and property damage.

[![Image 19: Peak wind gusts observed from Dec 17-18, 2023](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/CoastalStorm_Dec2023_PeakGusts.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/CoastalStorm_Dec2023_Rainfall.png)

**Peak wind gust analysis across southeast NC and northeast SC for December 17-18, 2023. Gusts just offshore were near hurricane-force (~70 mph)!**

**Tornado**

A coastal trough extending northward ahead of the storm shifted inland during the early afternoon of December 17 bringing warmer and moister air with it which led to sufficient [instability](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/mucape_effshear_121723_18Z.PNG) for severe thunderstorm development. Although most of the damaging winds were of the straight-line downburst variety, the[strong low-level helicity](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/esrh_121723_18Z.PNG)in place also led to a brief[tornado](https://twitter.com/EdPiotrowski/status/1736476349953380578) in Horry County, SC.

.Overview...A tornadic storm developed north of a strong coastal
low which moved northeast across eastern South Carolina.

.Socastee-Forestbrook...

Rating:                 EF1
Estimated Peak Wind:    95 mph
Path Length /statute/:  2.53 miles
Path Width /maximum/:   150 yards
Fatalities:             0
Injuries:               0

Start Date:             12/17/2023
Start Time:             01:16 PM EST
Start Location:         2 E Socastee / Horry County / SC
Start Lat/Lon:          33.6837 / -78.9737

End Date:               12/17/2023
End Time:               01:20 PM EST
End Location:           2 ESE Forestbrook / Horry County / SC
End Lat/Lon:            33.7081 / -78.9451

Survey Summary:
The tornado touched down south of Socastee Blvd between Everette
St and Tyner St, snapping several large trees and blowing off
portions of roofs from a few mobile homes. It moved north,
skipped across Socastee Blvd, and snapped several large pines
along Village Dr. Eight homes suffered moderate to major damage
as a result of falling trees. The storm cell continued north
across inaccessible property, and emerged near Folly Rd and
Wayland Circle. Significant damage was observed to several homes
and trees. Several trees were snapped or uprooted, and minor to
moderate damage was noted to roofs and siding. One mobile home
was pushed off its block foundation. The tornado appeared to lift
as it crossed the Intracoastal Waterway and touched down again on
the Arrowhead Country Club property. Numerous large hard and
softwood trees were snapped just south of the Flintlake
Apartments. Tree debris was blown into several apartments,
breaking windows and causing moderate roof and siding damage.

Damage upstream of the initial touchdown, along and south of
Palmetto Pointe Blvd, was straightline in nature and not the
result of a tornado. Additional wind damage occurred to the old
Waccamaw Mall at Fantasy Harbour. Portions of the facade were
blown off, in addition to several pieces of siding. A few bay
doors were blown in, and a large section of storefront wall was
buckled outward a few inches. A few nearby UPS and FedEx trucks
were blown over, in addition to a tractor trailer. This damage
appeared to be the result of straightline winds that occurred
after the tornado dissipated and the storm cell bowed
northeastward. Spotty tree damage was also observed on the
northeast side of Highway 501 in the River Oaks area.

EF5.....>200 mph

## **Overview**

A strengthening low pressure system in the eastern Gulf of America on December 16, 2023 moved northeast across Florida and along the Southeast U.S. coast December 17 and 18. Near hurricane-force wind gusts, significant rainfall and tidal flooding, and an EF-1 tornado occurred across portions of southeast NC,northeast SC and the adjacent Atlantic Ocean.

The storm was a ["nor'easter"](https://www.weather.gov/safety/winter-noreaster) -- a non-tropical low pressure system that produces strong northeast winds along the coastline. While nor'easters are not uncommon during the fall, winter, and early spring, this was a particularly strong one with [record low sea level pressure readings for December](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/research/roth/DecemberRecordLowSLPs.gif)(see below).Unlike tropical systems (e.g., tropical storms and hurricanes), nor'easters feed off the temperature differences between cold and warm air masses, which is why they are most common during cooler months when the land can cool down a lot more than the Atlantic Ocean.

**Record Low Sea Level Pressures Set for December:**

* Wilmington, NC (ILM) - 985.4 mb (29.10 in Hg)

* N Myrtle Beach, SC (CRE) - 988.1 mb (29.18 in Hg)

* Myrtle Beach, SC (MYR) - 989.2 mb (29.21 in Hg)[![Image 12](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/WPCanal.jpg)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/WPCanal.jpg)

## **Rainfall**

A surface [trough](https://forecast.weather.gov/glossary.php?word=Trough) along the coast along with[deep moisture](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/pwat_121723_18Z.PNG)and strong [mid-level moisture transport](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/h85mtrans_121723_18Z.PNG)led to abundant[moisture convergence](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/mconv_121723_18Z.PNG)and very heavy rainfall across much of the area. The heaviest rainfall was focused along the SC coast and led to significant flash flooding, especially in [Georgetown](https://twitter.com/ReedTimmerAccu/status/1736546082627141720?s=20) and Horry Counties where widespread totals of 6+"were observed with locally higher amounts of 10-15". Daily rainfall records were even set for December 17 at all 4 of our official climate sites: N. Myrtle Beach, SC (CRE) - 3.59", Florence, SC (FLO) - 2.39", Wilmington, NC (ILM) - 3.23" and Lumberton, NC (LBT) - 4.08".

## **Coastal Flooding**

The tidal forecast was definitely one of the most challenging aspects of this event. As is typical in such nor'easters, we anticipated a significant risk from coastal flooding but trying to pinpoint the exact water levels everywhere along the coast is always difficult, especially given the uncertainty regarding the storm's track/timing/strength. This is especially the case at our 3 Total Water Level (TWL) forecast sites - [Springmaid Pier in Myrtle Beach,SC](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/MROS1), [Johnnie Mercer's Pier in Wrightsville Beach, NC](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/JMPN7) and [along the Cape Fear River at Wilmington, NC](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/WLON7).

Persistent, strong north to northeast winds helped raise water levels along the coast prior to the storm's arrival from the south. Water levels then peaked during the afternoon on Sunday, December 17 around the time of the strongest onshore winds, although this was several hours after the highest astronomical tides. Thus, water levels could have been higher if the peak [storm surge](https://w1.weather.gov/glossary/index.php?word=storm+surge)occurred closer to high astronomical tide!The highest water level recorded at [Springmaid Pier](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/MROS1) was 9.97 ft above Mean Lower Low Water (MLLW) / 4.37 ft above Mean Higher High Water (MHHW), which was one of the highest tides on record at the time (and highest tide not related to a tropical cyclone!). At [Wilmington](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/WLON7), the tide peaked at 7.03 ft MLLW / 2.35 ft MHHW. However, the greatest surge occurred closer to low tide at [Wrightsville Beach](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/JMPN7) and thus, only minor coastal flooding levels were reached there. Ultimately, minor to moderate coastal flooding occurred across the area, with the greatest water levels south of Cape Fear, including [Pawleys Island, SC](https://twitter.com/PawleysIslandPD/status/1736432136419193085?s=20), [Myrtle Beach, SC](https://twitter.com/AndrewElswickWX/status/1736450832357261393?s=20), [N. Myrtle Beach, SC](https://twitter.com/accuweather/status/1736461314690896369?s=20),[Cherry Grove, SC](https://www.facebook.com/MeteorologistJamieArnold/posts/pfbid02yhUkYnFauGst5jeGfhMtqWCqpzgwhqHRm3dbKqVSW9x4DmGDW15FKsA64NJuZ1Gjl),[Ocean Isle Beach, NC](https://twitter.com/MaraMcJiltonTV/status/1736474115568017583?s=20)and [Southport, NC](https://www.facebook.com/brunswicksheriffNC/posts/pfbid02aHTSbRoJheZGjiHXdLkBSymyy6HN7hajZsy3my96EVBHVmEqZGTid4NrUz7LSgsWl).

## **Winds**

[Wind gusts](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=PNSILM&e=202312182051) reached tropical storm force (>=39 mph) across much of the region, a combination of pressure gradient winds and convective winds, as well as from a[gravity wave](https://w1.weather.gov/glossary/index.php?word=gravity%20wave)(around Florence, SC). The strong winds and heavy rainfall loosened up the soils and resulted in some downed trees/power lines and property damage.

[![Image 19: Peak wind gusts observed from Dec 17-18, 2023](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/CoastalStorm_Dec2023_PeakGusts.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/CoastalStorm_Dec2023_Rainfall.png)

**Peak wind gust analysis across southeast NC and northeast SC for December 17-18, 2023. Gusts just offshore were near hurricane-force (~70 mph)!**

**Tornado**

A coastal trough extending northward ahead of the storm shifted inland during the early afternoon of December 17 bringing warmer and moister air with it which led to sufficient [instability](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/mucape_effshear_121723_18Z.PNG) for severe thunderstorm development. Although most of the damaging winds were of the straight-line downburst variety, the[strong low-level helicity](https://www.weather.gov/images/ilm/events/CoastalStormDec2023/esrh_121723_18Z.PNG)in place also led to a brief[tornado](https://twitter.com/EdPiotrowski/status/1736476349953380578) in Horry County, SC.

...NWS Damage Survey for 12/17/2023 Tornado Event...

.Overview...A tornadic storm developed north of a strong coastal
low which moved northeast across eastern South Carolina.

.Socastee-Forestbrook...

Rating:                 EF1
Estimated Peak Wind:    95 mph
Path Length /statute/:  2.53 miles
Path Width /maximum/:   150 yards
Fatalities:             0
Injuries:               0

Start Date:             12/17/2023
Start Time:             01:16 PM EST
Start Location:         2 E Socastee / Horry County / SC
Start Lat/Lon:          33.6837 / -78.9737

End Date:               12/17/2023
End Time:               01:20 PM EST
End Location:           2 ESE Forestbrook / Horry County / SC
End Lat/Lon:            33.7081 / -78.9451

Survey Summary:
The tornado touched down south of Socastee Blvd between Everette
St and Tyner St, snapping several large trees and blowing off
portions of roofs from a few mobile homes. It moved north,
skipped across Socastee Blvd, and snapped several large pines
along Village Dr. Eight homes suffered moderate to major damage
as a result of falling trees. The storm cell continued north
across inaccessible property, and emerged near Folly Rd and
Wayland Circle. Significant damage was observed to several homes
and trees. Several trees were snapped or uprooted, and minor to
moderate damage was noted to roofs and siding. One mobile home
was pushed off its block foundation. The tornado appeared to lift
as it crossed the Intracoastal Waterway and touched down again on
the Arrowhead Country Club property. Numerous large hard and
softwood trees were snapped just south of the Flintlake
Apartments. Tree debris was blown into several apartments,
breaking windows and causing moderate roof and siding damage.

Damage upstream of the initial touchdown, along and south of
Palmetto Pointe Blvd, was straightline in nature and not the
result of a tornado. Additional wind damage occurred to the old
Waccamaw Mall at Fantasy Harbour. Portions of the facade were
blown off, in addition to several pieces of siding. A few bay
doors were blown in, and a large section of storefront wall was
buckled outward a few inches. A few nearby UPS and FedEx trucks
were blown over, in addition to a tractor trailer. This damage
appeared to be the result of straightline winds that occurred
after the tornado dissipated and the storm cell bowed
northeastward. Spotty tree damage was also observed on the
northeast side of Highway 501 in the River Oaks area.

&&

EF1.....86 to 110 mph
EF2.....111 to 135 mph
EF3.....136 to 165 mph
EF4.....166 to 200 mph
EF5.....>200 mph

# TRACKING THE TROPICS: Debby is a Category 1 hurricane barreling toward Florida, Carolinas

by: [Hannah Rahner](https://www.wbtw.com/author/hannah-rahner/ "Posts by Hannah Rahner")

Posted: Aug 4, 2024 / 11:14 PM EDT

Updated: Aug 4, 2024 / 11:35 PM EDT

by: [Hannah Rahner](https://www.wbtw.com/author/hannah-rahner/ "Posts by Hannah Rahner")

Posted: Aug 4, 2024 / 11:14 PM EDT

Updated: Aug 4, 2024 / 11:35 PM EDT

SHARE[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.wbtw.com%2Fweather-news%2Fhurricanecenter%2Ftracking-the-tropics-debby-is-a-category-1-hurricane-barreling-toward-florida-carolinas%2F&picture=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.wbtw.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2Fsites%2F22%2F2024%2F08%2Fslot0_d56d95.jpg%3Fw%3D900&title=TRACKING%20THE%20TROPICS%3A%20Debby%20is%20a%20Category%201%20hurricane%20barreling%20toward%20Florida%2C%20Carolinas&description=Hurricane%20Debby%20has%20organized%20significantly%20throughout%20the%20day%20and%20is%20now%20forecasted%20to%20strengthen%20to%20an%2085%20mph%20hurricane%20on%20Monday%20before%20making%20landfall%20near%20Tallahassee%2C%20Fla.%20almost%20a%20year%20after%20Hurricane%20Idalia%20roared%20ashore%20last%20year.)[](https://www.threads.net/intent/post?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.wbtw.com%2Fweather-news%2Fhurricanecenter%2Ftracking-the-tropics-debby-is-a-category-1-hurricane-barreling-toward-florida-carolinas%2F)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=TRACKING%20THE%20TROPICS%3A%20Debby%20is%20a%20Category%201%20hurricane%20barreling%20toward%20Florida%2C%20Carolinas&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.wbtw.com%2Fweather-news%2Fhurricanecenter%2Ftracking-the-tropics-debby-is-a-category-1-hurricane-barreling-toward-florida-carolinas%2F)[](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.wbtw.com%2Fweather-news%2Fhurricanecenter%2Ftracking-the-tropics-debby-is-a-category-1-hurricane-barreling-toward-florida-carolinas%2F&title=TRACKING%20THE%20TROPICS%3A%20Debby%20is%20a%20Category%201%20hurricane%20barreling%20toward%20Florida%2C%20Carolinas)[](mailto:?subject=TRACKING%20THE%20TROPICS%3A%20Debby%20is%20a%20Category%201%20hurricane%20barreling%20toward%20Florida%2C%20Carolinas&body=From%20WBTW%0A%0A%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.wbtw.com%2Fweather-news%2Fhurricanecenter%2Ftracking-the-tropics-debby-is-a-category-1-hurricane-barreling-toward-florida-carolinas%2F)

MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. (WBTW) — Debby is now a hurricane with winds at 75 mph. Debby has maintained its forward speed due north at 12 mph, but it will be slowly down soon after landfall in Florida tomorrow morning.

![Image 17](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot0_60c3fa.jpg?w=900)
Storm surge and coastal flooding will occur but the rainfall is the most profound impact to the Carolinas. Almost all of Florida’s Gulf Coast is under tropical alerts with hurricane warnings in effect for counties along the Big Bend and inland even up into southern Georgia.

![Image 18](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot0_adb3d3.jpg?w=900)
Storm surge along Florida’s Gulf Coast will be 6-10 feet from Ochlockonee River to Suwannee River (located in Florida’s Big Bend). Storm surge warnings are up for portions of coastal South Carolina with 2-4 feet of surge expected. From the National Weather Service in Charleston:

“A Storm Surge Warning means there is a danger of life-threatening inundation, from rising water moving inland from the coastline, somewhere within this area within the next 36 hours”.

There are no active tropical alerts for the Grand Strand at the moment. The storm surge warning is from Charleston County southward.

![Image 19](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot2_7d8e01.jpg?w=900)
There is not 100% agreement among the models, but the likely scenario has Debby stalling south of the Grand Strand and this will lead to persistent rainfall and onshore flow; which when prolonged will lead to coastal flooding, storm surge, and devastating beach erosion.

Debby will likely be a weaker tropical storm which will minimize the wind threat and therefore keep the storm surge at 1-3 feet.

![Image 20](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot1_367b00.jpg?w=900)
The outer rainbands will arrive along the Grand Strand tomorrow afternoon, but the greatest impacts with persistent heavy rain and 30+ mph winds Tuesday-Thursday. Rainfall and wind will be prolonged into Friday even possibly Saturday.

The Weather Prediction Center has the Grand Strand under a 15% chance of flash flooding tomorrow and this climbs to almost the entire area under a 40% threat of flooding and Myrtle Beach under a 70% chance on Tuesday. The outlook for Wednesday will likely be even worse.

![Image 21](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot0_a9c265.jpg?w=900)![Image 22](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot1_a1b400.jpg?w=900)
The rainfall estimate is 7-15 inches. This amount of rainfall is equivalent to Hurricane Matthew conditions which would push numerous rivers into moderate/major flood stage even after the storm has ended.

![Image 23](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot3_3143d4.jpg?w=900)
Each storm is unique. Matthew’s rainfall was so devastating because it was the tropical system to brought rainfall to the Carolinas in a couple of months, therefore soils which very wet when Matthew dropped 12-18 inches of rain.

# TRACKING THE TROPICS: Debby is a Category 1 hurricane barreling toward Florida, Carolinas

by: [Hannah Rahner](https://www.wbtw.com/author/hannah-rahner/ "Posts by Hannah Rahner")

Posted: Aug 4, 2024 / 11:14 PM EDT

Updated: Aug 4, 2024 / 11:35 PM EDT

by: [Hannah Rahner](https://www.wbtw.com/author/hannah-rahner/ "Posts by Hannah Rahner")

Posted: Aug 4, 2024 / 11:14 PM EDT

Updated: Aug 4, 2024 / 11:35 PM EDT

SHARE[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.wbtw.com%2Fweather-news%2Fhurricanecenter%2Ftracking-the-tropics-debby-is-a-category-1-hurricane-barreling-toward-florida-carolinas%2F&picture=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.wbtw.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2Fsites%2F22%2F2024%2F08%2Fslot0_d56d95.jpg%3Fw%3D900&title=TRACKING%20THE%20TROPICS%3A%20Debby%20is%20a%20Category%201%20hurricane%20barreling%20toward%20Florida%2C%20Carolinas&description=Hurricane%20Debby%20has%20organized%20significantly%20throughout%20the%20day%20and%20is%20now%20forecasted%20to%20strengthen%20to%20an%2085%20mph%20hurricane%20on%20Monday%20before%20making%20landfall%20near%20Tallahassee%2C%20Fla.%20almost%20a%20year%20after%20Hurricane%20Idalia%20roared%20ashore%20last%20year.)[](https://www.threads.net/intent/post?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.wbtw.com%2Fweather-news%2Fhurricanecenter%2Ftracking-the-tropics-debby-is-a-category-1-hurricane-barreling-toward-florida-carolinas%2F)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=TRACKING%20THE%20TROPICS%3A%20Debby%20is%20a%20Category%201%20hurricane%20barreling%20toward%20Florida%2C%20Carolinas&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.wbtw.com%2Fweather-news%2Fhurricanecenter%2Ftracking-the-tropics-debby-is-a-category-1-hurricane-barreling-toward-florida-carolinas%2F)[](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.wbtw.com%2Fweather-news%2Fhurricanecenter%2Ftracking-the-tropics-debby-is-a-category-1-hurricane-barreling-toward-florida-carolinas%2F&title=TRACKING%20THE%20TROPICS%3A%20Debby%20is%20a%20Category%201%20hurricane%20barreling%20toward%20Florida%2C%20Carolinas)[](mailto:?subject=TRACKING%20THE%20TROPICS%3A%20Debby%20is%20a%20Category%201%20hurricane%20barreling%20toward%20Florida%2C%20Carolinas&body=From%20WBTW%0A%0A%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.wbtw.com%2Fweather-news%2Fhurricanecenter%2Ftracking-the-tropics-debby-is-a-category-1-hurricane-barreling-toward-florida-carolinas%2F)

MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. (WBTW) — Debby is now a hurricane with winds at 75 mph. Debby has maintained its forward speed due north at 12 mph, but it will be slowly down soon after landfall in Florida tomorrow morning.

![Image 17](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot0_60c3fa.jpg?w=900)
Storm surge and coastal flooding will occur but the rainfall is the most profound impact to the Carolinas. Almost all of Florida’s Gulf Coast is under tropical alerts with hurricane warnings in effect for counties along the Big Bend and inland even up into southern Georgia.

![Image 18](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot0_adb3d3.jpg?w=900)
Storm surge along Florida’s Gulf Coast will be 6-10 feet from Ochlockonee River to Suwannee River (located in Florida’s Big Bend). Storm surge warnings are up for portions of coastal South Carolina with 2-4 feet of surge expected. From the National Weather Service in Charleston:

“A Storm Surge Warning means there is a danger of life-threatening inundation, from rising water moving inland from the coastline, somewhere within this area within the next 36 hours”.

There are no active tropical alerts for the Grand Strand at the moment. The storm surge warning is from Charleston County southward.

![Image 19](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot2_7d8e01.jpg?w=900)
There is not 100% agreement among the models, but the likely scenario has Debby stalling south of the Grand Strand and this will lead to persistent rainfall and onshore flow; which when prolonged will lead to coastal flooding, storm surge, and devastating beach erosion.

Debby will likely be a weaker tropical storm which will minimize the wind threat and therefore keep the storm surge at 1-3 feet.

![Image 20](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot1_367b00.jpg?w=900)
The outer rainbands will arrive along the Grand Strand tomorrow afternoon, but the greatest impacts with persistent heavy rain and 30+ mph winds Tuesday-Thursday. Rainfall and wind will be prolonged into Friday even possibly Saturday.

The Weather Prediction Center has the Grand Strand under a 15% chance of flash flooding tomorrow and this climbs to almost the entire area under a 40% threat of flooding and Myrtle Beach under a 70% chance on Tuesday. The outlook for Wednesday will likely be even worse.

![Image 21](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot0_a9c265.jpg?w=900)![Image 22](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot1_a1b400.jpg?w=900)
The rainfall estimate is 7-15 inches. This amount of rainfall is equivalent to Hurricane Matthew conditions which would push numerous rivers into moderate/major flood stage even after the storm has ended.

![Image 23](https://www.wbtw.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2024/08/slot3_3143d4.jpg?w=900)
Each storm is unique. Matthew’s rainfall was so devastating because it was the tropical system to brought rainfall to the Carolinas in a couple of months, therefore soils which very wet when Matthew dropped 12-18 inches of rain.

Hurricane Ian made landfall in Georgetown, South Carolina on Friday September 30, 2022 at 2:05pm as a category 1 storm and was downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone at 4:42pm with winds at 70mph. It moved through South Carolina at about 15 mph.

As of 7:00pm South Carolina had 180,604 power outages across the state.

Flooding was reported up to 5 – 7 feet, and inland flooding was 4 – 8 inches. A storm surge of 6.2 feet and a storm tide of 5.17 feet above Mean Higher High Water (MHHW) was observed at 1:36 p.m. Friday, September 30. This was that location’s third highest water level on record – far below the 8.77 feet recorded during Hurricane Hugo in 1989, but still enough to produce significant flooding.

The National Weather Service recorded 3.11 inches of rain in North Myrtle Beach, 2.12 in Myrtle Beach and 3.03 inches in Conway. Isaias nearly caused a record-breaking high tide of 10.18 feet at the Springmaid Pier.Heavy winds and gusts exceeding 50 miles per hour knocked out power lines and caused structural damage. The eye of the storm moved over Myrtle Beach with winds reaching 85 mph.

# What kind of damage did Idalia cause in SC? Take a look

 By [Patrick McCreless](https://www.thestate.com/profile/258886113/)

August 31, 2023 10:16 AM[![Image 6: Gift Icon](https://www.thestate.com/bl-yinzsoo/data/giftArticle/giftIcon.png)Gift Article](https://www.thestate.com/news/weather-news/article278814874.html)

Aug. 31, 2023.](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/public/latest-news/voarhl/picture278814969/alternates/LANDSCAPE_1200/idaliadamage-7.jpg)

 Portions of a roof lay scattered in the canals of Hog Inlet in North Myrtle Beach S.C. after a tornado damaged roofs near 56th Avenue North in North Myrtle Beach, S.C. Hurricane Idalia was downgraded to a tropical storm after hitting the gulf coast of Florida on Wednesday but brought heavy rains, coastal flooding and tornados to the South Carolina coastline. Aug. 31, 2023.  JASON LEE jlee@thesunnews.com

South Carolina counties along the coast were reeling from flooded streets, downed trees and the loss of power because of Idalia Thursday morning.

The tropical storm pummeled South Carolina on Wednesday, generating onshore winds of about 40 mph that pushed in water from the Atlantic, from Charleston to Myrtle Beach. Meanwhile, heavy rains further added to flooding problems in multiple counties.

According to the National Weather Service, all tropical storm warnings for the state had been canceled early Thursday morning as the storm pushed eastward.

Also, approximately [14,523 residents in South Carolina](https://poweroutage.us/area/state/south%20carolina)were without electricity as of 10:13 a.m. on Thursday.

Here’s a list of early reports of damage from across South Carolina.

### Charleston

Water breached the Charleston Battery, which is the seawall of Charleston, [the National Weather Service in Charleston](https://twitter.com/NWSCharlestonSC/status/1697026599814861232?s=20) stated on social media Wednesday. The NWS in Charleston also posted Wednesday that there was major coastal flooding reported in downtown Charleston and Edisto Beach.

![Image 8: A view of the Charleston Battery at high tide Wednesday.](https://www.thestate.com/public/latest-news/fr5mnl/picture278816679/alternates/FREE_1200/IMG_0738.JPG)

 A view of the Charleston Battery at high tide Wednesday. screenshot Courtesy of John Vinson

Tide levels reached over 9 feet in the Charleston Harbor. Also, the dunes were breached at Edisto and water flowed under homes and onto roads, the NWS posted.

Water levels in Charleston were the fifth highest ever reported in the city, based on records dating back to 1921, the NWS added.

### Myrtle Beach

According to [The Sun News](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/news/weather-news/article278809154.html), while the Grand Strand saw its fair share of rain and soggy streets, the main damage from Idalia was in the Cherry Grove area.

A possible tornado damaged a home late Wednesday evening. Another home lost its roof and there was some other cosmetic damage around the Cherry Grove area, along with damaged docks.

Some roads in Myrtle Beach remained barricaded Thursday morning because of flooding.

The Horry County Fire and Rescue responded to several calls of downed trees on roads and vehicles stuck in flooded roadways Wednesday evening, The Sun News states. Also, Horry County Police reported multiple hazards in roads, from structural debris to fallen trees and flooded cars.

![Image 9: Aynor High School’s parking lot saw significant flooding as Tropical Storm Idalia moved over the area on Aug. 30 and Aug. 31, 2023.](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/public/news/local/1hacwm/picture278814149/alternates/FREE_1200/Aynor%20High%20School%20Idalia)

 Aynor High School’s parking lot saw significant flooding as Tropical Storm Idalia moved over the area on Aug. 30 and Aug. 31, 2023. Adam Benson The Sun News 

### Beaufort County

Idalia left a trail of downed trees and coastal storm surge flooding, including at Sands Beach in Port Royal, but no major damage had been reported as of early Thursday, [according to the Island Packet](https://www.islandpacket.com/news/weather-news/article278787084.html).

The NWS had received received a report of 3.57 inches of rain in Beaufort County as of early Thursday. Also, storm surge of 2 to 4 feet was reported from Hunting Island in northern Beaufort County.

### Colleton County

The [Colleton County Fire and Rescue](https://www.facebook.com/search/top?q=colleton%20county%20eoc) reported that the county’s Emergency Operation Center received multiple damage reports Wednesday on primary and secondary roads, as well as on Interstate 95. Obstructions included downed trees, flooding and downed power lines and poles.

 By [Patrick McCreless](https://www.thestate.com/profile/258886113/)

August 31, 2023 10:16 AM[![Image 6: Gift Icon](https://www.thestate.com/bl-yinzsoo/data/giftArticle/giftIcon.png)Gift Article](https://www.thestate.com/news/weather-news/article278814874.html)

Hurricane Idalia was downgraded to a tropical storm after hitting the gulf coast of Florida on Wednesday but brought heavy rains, coastal flooding and tornados to the South Carolina coastline. Aug. 31, 2023.](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/public/latest-news/voarhl/picture278814969/alternates/LANDSCAPE_1200/idaliadamage-7.jpg)

 Portions of a roof lay scattered in the canals of Hog Inlet in North Myrtle Beach S.C. after a tornado damaged roofs near 56th Avenue North in North Myrtle Beach, S.C. Hurricane Idalia was downgraded to a tropical storm after hitting the gulf coast of Florida on Wednesday but brought heavy rains, coastal flooding and tornados to the South Carolina coastline. Aug. 31, 2023.  JASON LEE jlee@thesunnews.com

South Carolina counties along the coast were reeling from flooded streets, downed trees and the loss of power because of Idalia Thursday morning.

The tropical storm pummeled South Carolina on Wednesday, generating onshore winds of about 40 mph that pushed in water from the Atlantic, from Charleston to Myrtle Beach. Meanwhile, heavy rains further added to flooding problems in multiple counties.

According to the National Weather Service, all tropical storm warnings for the state had been canceled early Thursday morning as the storm pushed eastward.

Also, approximately [14,523 residents in South Carolina](https://poweroutage.us/area/state/south%20carolina)were without electricity as of 10:13 a.m. on Thursday.

Here’s a list of early reports of damage from across South Carolina.

### Charleston

Water breached the Charleston Battery, which is the seawall of Charleston, [the National Weather Service in Charleston](https://twitter.com/NWSCharlestonSC/status/1697026599814861232?s=20) stated on social media Wednesday. The NWS in Charleston also posted Wednesday that there was major coastal flooding reported in downtown Charleston and Edisto Beach.

![Image 8: A view of the Charleston Battery at high tide Wednesday.](https://www.thestate.com/public/latest-news/fr5mnl/picture278816679/alternates/FREE_1200/IMG_0738.JPG)

 A view of the Charleston Battery at high tide Wednesday. screenshot Courtesy of John Vinson

Tide levels reached over 9 feet in the Charleston Harbor. Also, the dunes were breached at Edisto and water flowed under homes and onto roads, the NWS posted.

Water levels in Charleston were the fifth highest ever reported in the city, based on records dating back to 1921, the NWS added.

### Myrtle Beach

According to [The Sun News](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/news/weather-news/article278809154.html), while the Grand Strand saw its fair share of rain and soggy streets, the main damage from Idalia was in the Cherry Grove area.

A possible tornado damaged a home late Wednesday evening. Another home lost its roof and there was some other cosmetic damage around the Cherry Grove area, along with damaged docks.

Some roads in Myrtle Beach remained barricaded Thursday morning because of flooding.

The Horry County Fire and Rescue responded to several calls of downed trees on roads and vehicles stuck in flooded roadways Wednesday evening, The Sun News states. Also, Horry County Police reported multiple hazards in roads, from structural debris to fallen trees and flooded cars.

![Image 9: Aynor High School’s parking lot saw significant flooding as Tropical Storm Idalia moved over the area on Aug. 30 and Aug. 31, 2023.](https://www.myrtlebeachonline.com/public/news/local/1hacwm/picture278814149/alternates/FREE_1200/Aynor%20High%20School%20Idalia)

 Aynor High School’s parking lot saw significant flooding as Tropical Storm Idalia moved over the area on Aug. 30 and Aug. 31, 2023. Adam Benson The Sun News 

### Beaufort County

Idalia left a trail of downed trees and coastal storm surge flooding, including at Sands Beach in Port Royal, but no major damage had been reported as of early Thursday, [according to the Island Packet](https://www.islandpacket.com/news/weather-news/article278787084.html).

The NWS had received received a report of 3.57 inches of rain in Beaufort County as of early Thursday. Also, storm surge of 2 to 4 feet was reported from Hunting Island in northern Beaufort County.

### Colleton County

The [Colleton County Fire and Rescue](https://www.facebook.com/search/top?q=colleton%20county%20eoc) reported that the county’s Emergency Operation Center received multiple damage reports Wednesday on primary and secondary roads, as well as on Interstate 95. Obstructions included downed trees, flooding and downed power lines and poles.

[Hurricane Hugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hugo "Hurricane Hugo") approaching South Carolina as a Category 4 hurricane on September 21, 1989

Since 1851, 132 [tropical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_cyclone "Tropical cyclone") or [subtropical cyclones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtropical_cyclone "Subtropical cyclone") have either directly or indirectly affected the state of [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina"), with the most recent being [Chantal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Chantal_(2025) "Tropical Storm Chantal (2025)") in [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Atlantic_hurricane_season "2025 Atlantic hurricane season").

SOUTH CAROLINA TROPICAL
CYCLONE CLIMATOLOGY

Understanding tropical cyclones is essential  to understanding  South Carolina's
climatology, especially as  coastal  communities  grow. However,  the  impacts of
these systems are not  limited to the coast. Inland  areas have been affected by
flooding, rain, high winds, and tornadoes.
From 1851 to 2025, 45 tropical cyclones
have made landfall on the South
Carolina coast. Of  these that have hit
the state's coast, only four made
landfall as major (Category 3+)
hurricanes. They are the 1893 Great
Charleston Hurricane, Hurricane Hazel
of 1954, Hurricane Gracie of 1959, and
Hurricane Hugo  of 1989. There are no
Category 5 hurricane landfalls on
record in South Carolina. One other
hurricane, the 1893 Sea Islands  hurricane, had the impact of a major hurricane in
South Carolina after making landfall in Georgia.
While the official Atlantic Hurricane Season runs from June 1 to November 30,
tropical cyclones  sometimes form outside  these  dates,  mainly  in  May  and
December. Thirteen  tropical cyclones  have  affected South  Carolina  during  May,
seven of which have occurred since 2007.
This  summary includes  a
statistical analysis of the
historical tropical
cyclones affecting the
Palmetto State.  It  also
contains  an  overview of
tropical cyclone  hazards,
brief narratives of notable
hurricanes that have
impacted South  Carolina,
and a timeline of tropical
cyclones that have hit  the
state since 1851.

SOUTH CAROLINA TROPICAL
CYCLONE TRACK DENSITY
This map includes the counts of the storms categorized by the National Hurricane
Center  as  either  formerly tropical extratropical storms,  tropical depressions,  tropical
storms, or hurricanes that have passed into  or through the state  from any  direction,
not just those making landfall on the coastline. This map does not include the tracks
of tropical cyclone remnants or the far-reaching impacts of  tropical cyclones  that
tracked outside the state. The map clearly shows that counties near the coast are
more frequently affected by tropical cyclones than counties in the Upstate.

Tropical cyclones can be hazardous for residents all over the state, even if landfall
does not  occur along the South Carolina coast. As a tropical cyclone moves inland,
it loses its strength since it is no longer over its fuel source, the warm ocean water.
Even in a weakened state, the remnants of these storms can produce heavy rain,
tornadoes, and strong winds in the state's interior.

HAZARDS
Inland Flooding
Flooding from heavy rain has been the leading
cause of tropical cyclone-related deaths since
2013, accounting for over half of such deaths.
Flooding rain from tropical cyclones does not
correlate  with the intensity of the tropical
storm or hurricane but rather the storm's
forward speed; slower-moving tropical
cyclones cause longer-lasting heavy rainfall.
Torrential rains can occur hundreds of miles
from the storm's center. Slow-moving Florence
of 2018 dropped more than 30 inches of rain
across portions of eastern North Carolina and
over 20 inches in Horry County, the most on
record for a tropical  cyclone in South Carolina.
Helene and Debby of 2024 produced historic
rainfall in the state, resulting in record river
crests. Debby was also a slow-mover, while
Helene was the second extreme  rain event
over a few days in the Upstate.

Tornadoes

Tornadoes produced by tropical cyclones form
in the outer rainbands, which can be hundreds
of miles away from the storm's center and are
most likely to occur in the northeastern
quadrant of the storm. More than half of
landfalling hurricanes  produce at least one
tornado. One of the most significant tornado
outbreaks recorded in South Carolina was
Hurricane Frances (2004), which made landfall
along the east coast of Florida. Thunderstorms
in the far-reaching  outer rainbands spawned
over 100 tornadoes across the Southeast,
including 46 in South Carolina. Most of the
tornadoes were relatively weak, rated F-0 or F  -
1 on the Fujita Scale in use at the time, but one
in Kershaw County was an F-3 that destroyed
buildings and mobile homes near Camden.

NOTABLE HURRICANES
August 28,  1893: The Sea Islands Hurricane

Telegraph  and telephone
communication capabilities
rapidly grew during the late
19th Century, enabling
warnings of approaching
severe weather to reach
densely populated areas.
However, warnings could not
reach more isolated
populations,  such as those
residing on the Sea Islands of
Georgia and South Carolina..

On August 28, 1893, a Category 3 hurricane made landfall at Ossabaw Island, Georgia, at high
tide before moving into South Carolina. It created an enormous storm surge that submerged
many of the Sea Islands. Winds estimated at 125 mph hit the Beaufort area, while winds were
estimated to be near 120 mph in Charleston. At least 2,000 South Carolinians died, and the
hurricane  caused $334.1 million (inflation-adjusted to 2023) of damage. It was the first of two
major hurricanes to affect South Carolina in 1893. The 1893 Charleston Hurricane hit as a
Category 3 storm near McClellanville on October 18, causing more extensive damage.
July 14, 1916: The 1916 Charleston Hurricane

This was a Category  2 hurricane  at landfall near
Awendaw, with winds estimated at 105  mph. It
drifted northwestward over eastern South
Carolina, which resulted in record rainfall for the
time and widespread flooding. A weather station
in Effingham  (Florence County) recorded 13.25
inches of rain in 24 hours. This hurricane caused
about $282 million (inflation-adjusted  to  2023) in
damages, destroying over 700,000 acres of
crops and causing the most extensive flooding of
the Santee River System since records began in
1840. A tropical cyclone that affected the state a
few days earlier was partly responsible for the
historic flooding in the Upstate. Rainfall and
flooding were also historic in western North
Carolina. The flood damaged the original
Catawba Dam in York County. It was rebuilt as
the Lake Wylie Dam in 1924.
