Appendix  A: Recent Changes

Research on past storms has led to minor changes to the historical record of hurricane landfalls
and impacts in South Carolina. First, a review of the 2008 hurricane  season conducted in late
2025 found that Tropical  Storm Cristobal that year did not have enough effect on South
Carolina to be counted as a tropical  storm impact. Second, a review of the 1987 hurricane
season found that Tropical Depression Nine did not make landfall in South Carolina; instead,
the center moved ashore near Ocean Isle Beach, North Carolina. These changes reduce the
number of tropical storm impacts in South Carolina by one and reduce the number of tropical
depression  landfalls by one.

During the 2025 hurricane season, South Carolina experienced one tropical cyclone, Tropical
Storm Chantal. Chantal made landfall as a tropical storm in South Carolina, increasing the count
of tropical  storm landfalls and impacts by one each.

2024 brought two tropical cyclones to South Carolina: Debby and Helene, both highly
impactful. Helene, which made landfall as a major hurricane in Florida, was ruled by the
Hurricane Research Division of the Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory not
to be a hurricane  impact in South Carolina. The State Climatology Office ruled it to be a high-
end tropical storm impact. Debby was a hurricane  over the Gulf as it made landfall in Florida. It
made a second landfall in South Carolina. So, for 2024, South Carolina received one tropical
storm landfall and two tropical storm impacts.

Two tropical cyclones affected South Carolina in 2023: Idalia and Ophelia. Idalia made landfall
in Florida as a major hurricane, then brought tropical storm conditions to parts of South
Carolina. Ophelia formed north of the Bahamas in September 2022 and made landfall in North
Carolina near Emerald Isle. It caused heavy rainfall in South Carolina, but no damaging winds,
storm surge, or tornadoes. For 2023, the Climatology Office ruled that South Carolina received
a tropical storm impact from Idalia and a tropical depression impact from Ophelia.

In 2022, South Carolina felt the direct effects of three tropical cyclones: Colin, Ian and Nicole.
Colin formed off the South Carolina coast, reached tropical storm intensity near Hunting Island,
and was counted as a tropical storm impact and landfall for the state. Ian was a major hurricane
at landfall in Florida. It crossed Central Florida and moved over the Atlantic before making
landfall as a Category 1 hurricane  near Pawleys Island. It was a Category 1 hurricane landfall and
impact for South Carolina. Nicole formed east of the Bahamas, hit Florida as a hurricane, then
moved west of South Carolina before dissipating. Nicole caused a small storm surge that led to
coastal flooding in the Lowcountry and widespread heavy rainfall in South Carolina. However, it
did not cause winds of at least tropical storm force, so the Climatology Office ruled it to be a
tropical depression impact. In total for 2023, South Carolina received one tropical depression
impact, one tropical storm impact, and one Category 1 hurricane impact, with one tropical storm
landfall and one Category 1 hurricane landfall.

These changes from storms that hit the state in recent years, along with changes resulting from
reviews and errors discovered, have led to minor adjustments to the statistics for hurricane
impacts and landfalls for this edition.

[PDF page 22]
Appendix  B: Methodology  For
Determining  Tropical Cyclone Impacts

When the center of a tropical cyclone moves onto land, the storm's landfall occurs at that
location. However, tropical cyclones are large weather features with a typical diameter of about
300 miles. Because of their size, tropical cyclones can have major impacts on areas far from
where landfall occurs. A tropical cyclone impact is a term used to describe the effect that a
tropical cyclone has, which is independent of where the storm made landfall or its intensity at
the time. Some storms, such as Hurricane Helene of 1958, do not make landfall in the United
States but still impact one or more states. Helene had a Category 3 impact on North Carolina
and a tropical storm impact on South Carolina.

Judging the impact of a tropical cyclone on a given state can be challenging, sometimes
requiring in-depth research. It is often tough to determine the impact of a weaker storm or one
that occurred in the distant past.

Researchers at the Hurricane Research Division of the Atlantic Oceanographic and
Meteorological  Laboratory in Virginia Key, Florida, have already done some of this work. They
have analyzed the hurricanes  that have affected the United States and assigned hurricane
landfall points and impacts for each state for every hurricane  in the historical records. They
have also generated a list of landfalling tropical storms in the United States.

The State Climatology Office accepts this work as the best documentation  on hurricanes  that have
made landfall in South Carolina or have had the impact of a Category 1 or higher hurricane  in the
state. We also consider this work the best documentation of landfalling tropical storms. However,
this dataset only covers about 15 percent of the tropical cyclones and formerly tropical extratropical
storms known to have impacted South Carolina.

A project that began in 2018 with the work of a Climatology Office intern has been expanded to
provide a more reliable and well-documented list of tropical cyclone impacts for tropical storm  -  and
tropical depression-level events, as well as for formerly tropical extratropical storms that impacted
South Carolina.

There are a few criteria for crediting a storm with causing tropical storm impact in South Carolina.
The first is that it made landfall as a tropical storm in South Carolina, or that the storm's track in the
HURDAT2 database had a point of tropical storm intensity within South Carolina. The second is that
research conducted by the SC State Climatology Office found that sustained tropical-storm  -force
winds occurred in South Carolina as the storm passed through or near the state. A third is that the
storm's radius of tropical-storm  -force  winds in the HURDAT2 database, where  available, covers  a
part of the state. Another criterion, mainly used for storms with no radius of winds available in
HURDAT2, is that the tropical cyclone passed within 20 nautical miles of South Carolina while a
tropical storm, or that a hurricane's center passed within 60 nautical miles of South Carolina.

SOUTH CAROLINA TROPICAL
CYCLONE CLIMATOLOGY

Understanding tropical cyclones is essential  to understanding  South Carolina's
climatology, especially as  coastal  communities  grow. However,  the  impacts of
these systems are not  limited to the coast. Inland  areas have been affected by
flooding, rain, high winds, and tornadoes.
From 1851 to 2025, 45 tropical cyclones
have made landfall on the South
Carolina coast. Of  these that have hit
the state's coast, only four made
landfall as major (Category 3+)
hurricanes. They are the 1893 Great
Charleston Hurricane, Hurricane Hazel
of 1954, Hurricane Gracie of 1959, and
Hurricane Hugo  of 1989. There are no
Category 5 hurricane landfalls on
record in South Carolina. One other
hurricane, the 1893 Sea Islands  hurricane, had the impact of a major hurricane in
South Carolina after making landfall in Georgia.
While the official Atlantic Hurricane Season runs from June 1 to November 30,
tropical cyclones  sometimes form outside  these  dates,  mainly  in  May  and
December. Thirteen  tropical cyclones  have  affected South  Carolina  during  May,
seven of which have occurred since 2007.
This  summary includes  a

Appendix  A: Recent Changes

Research on past storms has led to minor changes to the historical record of hurricane landfalls
and impacts in South Carolina. First, a review of the 2008 hurricane  season conducted in late
2025 found that Tropical  Storm Cristobal that year did not have enough effect on South
Carolina to be counted as a tropical  storm impact. Second, a review of the 1987 hurricane
season found that Tropical Depression Nine did not make landfall in South Carolina; instead,
the center moved ashore near Ocean Isle Beach, North Carolina. These changes reduce the
number of tropical storm impacts in South Carolina by one and reduce the number of tropical
depression  landfalls by one.

During the 2025 hurricane season, South Carolina experienced one tropical cyclone, Tropical
Storm Chantal. Chantal made landfall as a tropical storm in South Carolina, increasing the count
of tropical  storm landfalls and impacts by one each.

2024 brought two tropical cyclones to South Carolina: Debby and Helene, both highly
impactful. Helene, which made landfall as a major hurricane in Florida, was ruled by the
Hurricane Research Division of the Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory not
to be a hurricane  impact in South Carolina. The State Climatology Office ruled it to be a high-
end tropical storm impact. Debby was a hurricane  over the Gulf as it made landfall in Florida. It
made a second landfall in South Carolina. So, for 2024, South Carolina received one tropical
storm landfall and two tropical storm impacts.

in Florida as a major hurricane, then brought tropical storm conditions to parts of South
Carolina. Ophelia formed north of the Bahamas in September 2022 and made landfall in North
Carolina near Emerald Isle. It caused heavy rainfall in South Carolina, but no damaging winds,
storm surge, or tornadoes. For 2023, the Climatology Office ruled that South Carolina received
a tropical storm impact from Idalia and a tropical depression impact from Ophelia.

Colin formed off the South Carolina coast, reached tropical storm intensity near Hunting Island,
and was counted as a tropical storm impact and landfall for the state. Ian was a major hurricane
at landfall in Florida. It crossed Central Florida and moved over the Atlantic before making
landfall as a Category 1 hurricane  near Pawleys Island. It was a Category 1 hurricane landfall and
impact for South Carolina. Nicole formed east of the Bahamas, hit Florida as a hurricane, then
moved west of South Carolina before dissipating. Nicole caused a small storm surge that led to
coastal flooding in the Lowcountry and widespread heavy rainfall in South Carolina. However, it
did not cause winds of at least tropical storm force, so the Climatology Office ruled it to be a
tropical depression impact. In total for 2023, South Carolina received one tropical depression
impact, one tropical storm impact, and one Category 1 hurricane impact, with one tropical storm
landfall and one Category 1 hurricane landfall.

These changes from storms that hit the state in recent years, along with changes resulting from
reviews and errors discovered, have led to minor adjustments to the statistics for hurricane
impacts and landfalls for this edition.

[PDF page 22]
Appendix  B: Methodology  For
Determining  Tropical Cyclone Impacts

When the center of a tropical cyclone moves onto land, the storm's landfall occurs at that
location. However, tropical cyclones are large weather features with a typical diameter of about
300 miles. Because of their size, tropical cyclones can have major impacts on areas far from
where landfall occurs. A tropical cyclone impact is a term used to describe the effect that a
tropical cyclone has, which is independent of where the storm made landfall or its intensity at
the time. Some storms, such as Hurricane Helene of 1958, do not make landfall in the United
States but still impact one or more states. Helene had a Category 3 impact on North Carolina
and a tropical storm impact on South Carolina.

Judging the impact of a tropical cyclone on a given state can be challenging, sometimes
requiring in-depth research. It is often tough to determine the impact of a weaker storm or one
that occurred in the distant past.

Researchers at the Hurricane Research Division of the Atlantic Oceanographic and
Meteorological  Laboratory in Virginia Key, Florida, have already done some of this work. They
have analyzed the hurricanes  that have affected the United States and assigned hurricane
landfall points and impacts for each state for every hurricane  in the historical records. They
have also generated a list of landfalling tropical storms in the United States.

made landfall in South Carolina or have had the impact of a Category 1 or higher hurricane  in the
state. We also consider this work the best documentation of landfalling tropical storms. However,
this dataset only covers about 15 percent of the tropical cyclones and formerly tropical extratropical
storms known to have impacted South Carolina.

A project that began in 2018 with the work of a Climatology Office intern has been expanded to
provide a more reliable and well-documented list of tropical cyclone impacts for tropical storm  -  and
tropical depression-level events, as well as for formerly tropical extratropical storms that impacted
South Carolina.

There are a few criteria for crediting a storm with causing tropical storm impact in South Carolina.
The first is that it made landfall as a tropical storm in South Carolina, or that the storm's track in the
HURDAT2 database had a point of tropical storm intensity within South Carolina. The second is that
research conducted by the SC State Climatology Office found that sustained tropical-storm  -force
winds occurred in South Carolina as the storm passed through or near the state. A third is that the
storm's radius of tropical-storm  -force  winds in the HURDAT2 database, where  available, covers  a
part of the state. Another criterion, mainly used for storms with no radius of winds available in
HURDAT2, is that the tropical cyclone passed within 20 nautical miles of South Carolina while a
tropical storm, or that a hurricane's center passed within 60 nautical miles of South Carolina.

affecting South Carolina but not causing sustained winds of tropical storm force or higher. The

landfalling tropical depression in South Carolina, a tropical cyclone that passes over the state at
tropical depression intensity after making landfall elsewhere, or one that passes near South
Carolina but causes notable impacts in terms of storm surge flooding, flooding rainfall, or tornadoes.

[PDF page 24]
Some subjectivity arises when a tropical cyclone passes farther  from South Carolina. Some of
these were counted as impacts because they had clear and notable effects on the state, such
as heavy rainfall and flooding or a tornado outbreak. Those with limited impacts, such as
causing less than an inch of rainfall, were not counted as an impact. One special case is
Hurricane Joaquin of 2015, which was counted as a tropical depression impact due to its role in

Our database includes one additional category of
impacts: those from extratropical storms that were

Just a little reminder here as we close in on Hurricane Season. On average, Myrtle Beach can expect to have a tropical storm pass within 50 miles every 2 years and a Category 1 hurricane every 7 years. Of course we’ve seen much more activity than that going back to 2016. This is one of my favorite maps ever - all tropical storms and hurricanes since 1851! It’s easy to see we’re in the ‘hot zone’.

## **SC Lowcountry/****GA Coastal Empire Tropical Cyclone History**

**Updated: 10/14/24**

The following data is mainly based on the official Atlantic basin tropical cyclone (TC) database (HURDAT), which includes known tropical depressions (TD), tropical storms (TS) and hurricanes (H)back to 1851. Refer to the _[National Hurricane Center data archive page](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/)and \_NOAA \\_Historical\\_ Hurricane Track \\_s\\_ website\_ for more information \_.\__

_\_More local tropical cyclone statistics can be found [here](https://www.weather.gov/media/chs/misc/NWS\\_CHS\\_Tropical\\_Quick\\_Facts.pdf).\__

**2019 Climatological Study:**

*   _All TCs_: 
    *   Since official records began in 1851 through 2018, 309 TCs tracked through a[domain](https://www.weather.gov/images/chs/tropical/study_domain_map.jpg) roughly centered around the [NWS Charleston, SC County Warning Area (CWA)](https://www.weather.gov/images/chs/misc/chs_cwa.jpg), which runs from Charleston County, SC to McIntosh County, GA.
        *   Most TCs occurred during the typically busier period in the Atlantic basin from August through October, but June and July were also fairly active followed by May and November. The earliest TC was a TS that passed offshore in February 1952. Note that the 10 TCs that spanned 2 different months were counted twice (once for each month).
        *   There are general increasing decadal trends in total TCs and TD but general decreasing decadal trends in TS, H, and MH. This could at least partially be explained by better observations of weaker systems over time. There also appears to be cycles of TCs, especially H, likely associated with the [Atlantic Multi-decadal Oscillation](https://www.noaa.gov/stories/atlantic-high-activity-eras-what-does-it-mean-for-hurricane-season).
        *   There is a general increasing trend of early (prior to June) and late (after October) season TCs, possibly related to improved observations over time.
        *   From 1950 to 2018, more TCs occurred during "cool" [El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)](https://www.climate.gov/enso) conditions (i.e.,La Nina) compared to "warm" ENSO conditions (i.e., El Nino). However, early in the season more TC occurred during El Nino conditions. Also, all 7 of the major (Cat 3+) hurricanes occurred during either La Nina or neutral ENSO conditions. Furthermore, there was a slight preference for more(and stronger) TCs during moderate-strong La Nina conditions compared to moderate-strong El Nino conditions.

*   _Landfalling TCs:_
    *   Since official records began in 1851 through 2018, 41 TCs made landfall in the [NWS Charleston, SC CWA](https://www.weather.gov/images/chs/misc/chs_cwa.jpg). 
        *   25 TCs were H, 9 were TS, and 7 were TD.
        *   17 TCs made landfall in Charleston County, SC, 9 in Beaufort County, SC,6 in Chatham County, GA, 4 in McIntosh County, GA, 3 in Liberty County, GA, and 2 in Colleton County, SC.
        *   Most landfalls occurred in August (12) and September (12), with the earliest landfalls (2) in May and the latest landfalls (7) in October.
        *   There has been a general upward trend in the number of weaker TCs making landfall (although this could at least partly be due to increasingly better observations over time) and a general downward trend in the number of major (Cat 3-5)hurricane landfalls.
        *   From 1950 to 2018, the most (9) landfalling TCs occurred during "neutral" [El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)](https://www.climate.gov/enso) conditions, including both major hurricanes(Gracie-1959 and Hugo-1989). In addition, roughly the same number of landfalls occurred during"warm" ENSO (i.e., El Nino) conditions (5) versus "cold" ENSO (i.e., La Nina) conditions (4), with a majority of these during "weak" El Nino/La Nina conditions.
        *   From 1950 to 2018, there was a slight preference for TCs to make landfall during the positive phase of the [North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO)](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/teleconnections/nao/)rather than during the negative phase.
        *   From 1950 to 2018, there was no preference for TCs to make landfall during either the positive or negative phases of the [Arctic Oscillation (AO)](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/teleconnections/ao/).

**Notable Storms:**

**Pre-1800**
1686 Sep 4-5"Spanish Repulse"Likely made landfall near Charleston causing extensive damage to ships, trees, crops, houses and livestock, and killed many people. After the storm, the Spanish aborted an invasion and turned back to FL.
1700 Sep 14"Rising Sun"Likely made landfall north of Charleston causing severe storm surge flooding despite winds shifting just before high tide, damage to several ships, including the 800-ton Scottish ship "Rising Sun", and 100+ deaths.
1713 Sep 16-17"Great Storm"Extremely destructive hurricane made landfall north of Charleston causing significant property damage and at least 70 deaths.
1722 Sep 19-21 Likely made landfall near Savannah causing significant flooding with the Savannah River over-spilling its banks.
1728 Aug 13-14 Likely made landfall just south of Charleston causing significant damage to ships, houses, wharfs, bridges and crops.
1752 Sep 13-15"Great Hurricane"Very strong (but likely small) hurricane made landfall just south of Charleston near high tide producing severe storm surge flooding (~17 ft MLW at Charleston), much property/crop/livestock damage and at least 95 deaths. It is likely the worst storm to ever hit Charleston. The storm occurred around the transition from the Julian to Gregorian calendars.
1783 Oct 6-8 Strong hurricane tracked along the coast causing significant property damage but not as much flooding as the 1752 storm.
**1800s**
1804 Sep 6-8 Large, violent (likely Cat 3 or 4) hurricane moved north near the GA coast before likely moving inland over southern SC. Produced significant wind/water damage around Charleston and killed hundreds of people.
1811 Sep 8-10 Hurricane likely made landfall south of Charleston causing a tornado which caused a lot of damage in the city.
1813 Aug 27 Brief but violent hurricane caused significant property damage and storm surge flooding similar to the 1752 storm and worse than the 1804 storm.
1822 Sep 27 Landfall just north of Charleston, SC as a small likely Cat 3 hurricane producing severe damage, mainly around the Santee River.
**Official Records Begin in 1851**

**_**Storms highlighted in red made landfall in the NWS Charleston County Warning Area (CWA)**_**
[1854](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1854.html)Sep 7-9"Great Carolina"Landfall just south of Savannah, GA as a large Cat 3 hurricane and then slowly tracked just east of Statesboro, GA as a Cat 1 hurricane before weakening to a TS as it crossed the Savannah River into Allendale County, SC. Although most of the significant wind damage was near/south of Charleston, SC, substantial storm surge flooding occurred well northward along the SC coast ruining many crops.
[1867](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1867.html)Jun 21-23 _*****Earliest landfalling hurricane in the NWS Charleston CWA*****_ Landfall at Isle of Palms, SC on June 22 as a Cat 1 hurricane and then weakened to a TS before moving through the Pee Dee and into central NC.
[1874](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1874.html)Sep 27-28 Landfall on Seabrook Island, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane. Produced downed telegraph lines and extensive wharf/crop damage in Charleston along with 2 deaths.
[1878](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1878.html)Sep 10-12 Landfall just south of Charleston, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane. Produced significant crop damage.
[1881](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1881.html)Aug 26-28 Landfall just south of Savannah, GA as a Cat 2 hurricane with winds ~105 mph before moving west into central GA and weakening into a TS. Produced significant surge flooding, property/crop damage and 700 U.S. deaths.
[1884](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1884.html)Sep 9-13 Landfall south of Savannah, GA on St. Catherine's Island as a TS. Weakened to a TD over land and re-curved out to sea off the SC coast before re-strengthening to a TS.
[1885](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1885.html)Aug 24-25 Landfall at Kiawah Island, SC as a Cat 2 hurricane causing significant damage along the GA/SC coasts northward through around Pawley's Island, SC and at least 21 deaths.
[1893](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1893.html)Aug 27-28"Great Sea Islands"_*****Earliest landfalling major hurricane in the NWS Charleston CWA*****_ Landfall just south of Savannah, GA on August 28 as a very large Cat 3 hurricane with peak winds near 115 mph and minimum pressure of 954 mb. Moved north-northeast through the SC Midlands and weakened to a Cat 1 hurricane before reaching Columbia, SC. The storm tide along the coast was catastrophic, a combination of the ~16 foot storm surge and the high astronomical tides. Significant wind/water damage occurred northward through around Charleston and [at least 1,000 (possibly 2,000+) people were killed](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/pdf/nws-nhc-6.pdf)in the U.S.. Fortunately, Savannah was spared complete inundation and less damage/deaths occurred in Charleston compared to the 1885 storm. However, the storm essentially marked the beginning of the end of rice cultivation and the phosphate industry in the region.
[1893](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1893.html)Oct 12-13 Moved northeast off the coasts of GA before making landfall along the SC coast just north of Charleston as a compact Cat 3 hurricane with 120 mph winds and minimum central pressure of 955 mb. Produced significant flooding due to already wet ground from previous storms.
[1894](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1894.html)Sep 26-27 Landfall on Hilton Head Island, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane before moving northeast and passing just west of Charleston with winds around 80 mph.
[1896](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1896.html)Sep 29 Tracked through southeast GA as a Cat 2/3 hurricane and through southeast SC as a Cat 1/2 hurricane. Produced significant wind damage around Savannah, GA and Beaufort, SC.
[1898](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1898.html)Aug 30-31 Landfall on Hilton Head Island, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane. Produced significant wind damage around Savannah and saltwater from the storm surge wrecked rice crops along the Savannah and Ogeechee Rivers.
[1898](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1898.html)Oct 1-3 Landfall on Cumberland Island, GA as a Cat 4 hurricane with winds near 130 mph. Moved northwest into central GA and weakened to a Cat 1 hurricane over Telfair County and then to a TS southwest of Macon. Produced a storm tide near 20 feet on Jekyll Island (with some significant flooding even around Savannah, GA), significant property damage across southeast GA and 179 U.S. deaths.
**1900s**
[1911](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1911.html)Aug 27-30 Landfall on Hilton Head Island, SC as a Cat 2 hurricane with winds near 100 mph. Moved slowly westward and weakened into a TS before reaching Statesboro, GA. Wind gusts reached 110 mph in Beaufort, SC, 96 mph in Savannah, GA, 95 mph on Edisto Island, SC and 94 mph at Charleston, SC (before the Weather Bureau's anemometer broke) causing many trees, power lines, and telegraph lines to fall. A significant storm surge produced extensive flood damage, especially from around Beaufort to Charleston. Much of the rice crops were destroyed, effectively ending the region's rice industry.
[1912](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1912.html)Jul 14-16 Landfall near Altamaha Sound, GA as a TS. Slowly moved west across southern GA producing heavy rain.
[1912](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1912.html)Sep 5-6 TS moved southwest off the SC coast before weakening into a TD and then making landfall on Ossabaw Island, GA.
[1913](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1913.html)Oct 7-10 Landfall on Cape Island, SC just north of Charleston as a Cat 1 hurricane. Produced heavy rain, especially in northeast SC, including 4"+ at Charleston.
[1916](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1916.html)May 15-16 _*****Earliest landfalling tropical storm in the NWS Charleston CWA*****_ Landfall on Fripp Island, SC as a TS on May 16.
[1916](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1916.html)Jul 13-15 Landfall at Bulls Bay, SC as a compact Cat 2 hurricane. The storm moved slowly and produced very heavy rain which caused severe river flooding. In fact, the Santee River at [Jamestown](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/jams1) observed the highest water level on record. Damage was most significant north of Charleston and likely the worst in that area since the 1822 hurricane.
[1916](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1916.html)Oct 3-5 Landfall on Sapelo Island, GA as a TS.
[1927](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1927.html)Oct 2-3 Landfall near Edisto Beach, SC as a TS.
[1928](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1928.html)Sep 18"Lake Okeechobee"Landfall between Beaufort, SC and Charleston, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane. Produced some wind damage, mainly downed trees and power/phone lines, 1 1"+ of rain in Savannah, GA which caused significant flooding and ~$1 million in damage in Charleston.
[1940](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1940.html)Aug 10-13 Landfall near Hilton Head Island, SC as a Cat 2 hurricane with winds near 100 mph. Produced significant storm surge, 10+ inches of [rain](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/sehrcn1940.html)(mostly across SC).
[1945](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1945.html)Sep 16-17 Landfall near the GA/SC border as a TS. Produced gusts near 90 mph at Paris Island, SC, moderate flooding, and tornadoes with $6-7 million damage.
[1947](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1947.html)Oct 14-16 Landfall on Ossabaw Island, GA just south of Savannah as a Cat 2 hurricane with winds near 105 mph. The lowest pressure at Savannah was 28.77 in Hg (974 mb), which is the 3rd lowest on record.
1950 Sep 6-7 Easy TD moved through southern GA. Produced [very heavy rainfall](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/easy1950.html), especially across coastal GA where 15+ inches fell (Savannah, GA recorded 16" inches).
[1952](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1952.html)Aug 30-31 Able Landfall near Beaufort, SC as a Cat 2 hurricane with sustained winds near 100 mph and minimum central pressure near 980 mb. [1953](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1953.html)Aug 31-Sep 1 TS approached the GA coast but weakened into a TD before making landfall south of Savannah, GA. The storm then moved inland through southeast GA and dissipated over central GA.
[1954](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1954.html)Oct 14-15[Hazel](https://www.weather.gov/ilm/HurricaneHazelAnniversary)Brushed the SC Lowcountry and made landfall near the SC/NC border as a Cat 4 hurricane with sustained winds near 130 mph, the strongest storm on record to make landfall that far north. Caused 95 deaths in the U.S. and was one of the worst storms on record in SC with significant damage, mainly from Pawleys Island northward.
[1959](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1959.html)Jul 4-9[Cindy](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/storm_wallets/atlantic/atl1959/cindy/)Landfall just north of Charleston, SC near Bulls Bay as a Cat 1 hurricane with winds near 75 mph winds. 64 mph winds were recorded at McClellanville along with 1 death. [1959](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1959.html)Sep 28-30[Gracie](https://www.weather.gov/media/chs/events/HurricaneGracie1959.pdf)Landfall near Beaufort, SC as a Cat 4 hurricane with sustained winds near 130 mph and minimum pressure of 951 mb. Although a significant storm surge occurred (~9 feet at Charleston Harbor), the resulting flooding would have been much worse if the storm hit at high tide instead of low tide. The highest recorded storm tide was ~12 feet above mean low water (MLW) at Edisto Beach, SC. The relatively slow speed of the storm helped cause extensive wind/flooding damage across southeast SC, mainly in the Beaufort to Charleston corridor, along with 10 deaths in GA and SC. For more info, check out the [NHC archive](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/storm_wallets/atlantic/atl1959/gracie/).

[1971](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1971.html)Sep 10-11 Landfall near Charleston, SC as a TD and then dissipated before moving west into GA.
[1976](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1976.html)Aug 19-21[Dottie](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/storm_wallets/atlantic/atl1976-prelim/dottie/)Landfall near Charleston, SC as a TS before dissipating north of Lake Moultrie.
[1979](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1979.html)Jun 15-16 TD approached the central SC coast from the south and made landfall near Kiawah Island before dissipating east of Columbia. [1979](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1979.html)Sep 4-5[David](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/storm_wallets/atlantic/atl1979-prelim/david/)Landfall on Sapelo Island, GA as a Cat 1 hurricane with winds ~90 mph. [1981](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1981.html)Jul 3 TD moved north along the FL east coast and made landfall on Fripp Island, SC.
[1985](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1985.html)Jul 24-25[Bob](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/storm_wallets/atlantic/atl1985-prelim/bob/)Landfall on Fripp Island, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane. [1988](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1988.html)Aug 28[Chris](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/storm_wallets/atlantic/atl1988-prelim/chris/)Landfall near Savannah, GA as a TS. Produced [heavy rainfall](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/chris1988.html) (~3 inches over eastern SC).

## **SC Lowcountry/****GA Coastal Empire Tropical Cyclone History**

**Updated: 10/14/24**

The following data is mainly based on the official Atlantic basin tropical cyclone (TC) database (HURDAT), which includes known tropical depressions (TD), tropical storms (TS) and hurricanes (H)back to 1851. Refer to the _[National Hurricane Center data archive page](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/)and \_NOAA \\_Historical\\_ Hurricane Track \\_s\\_ website\_ for more information \_.\__

_\_More local tropical cyclone statistics can be found [here](https://www.weather.gov/media/chs/misc/NWS\\_CHS\\_Tropical\\_Quick\\_Facts.pdf).\__

**2019 Climatological Study:**

*   _All TCs_: 
    *   Since official records began in 1851 through 2018, 309 TCs tracked through a[domain](https://www.weather.gov/images/chs/tropical/study_domain_map.jpg) roughly centered around the [NWS Charleston, SC County Warning Area (CWA)](https://www.weather.gov/images/chs/misc/chs_cwa.jpg), which runs from Charleston County, SC to McIntosh County, GA.
        *   Most TCs occurred during the typically busier period in the Atlantic basin from August through October, but June and July were also fairly active followed by May and November. The earliest TC was a TS that passed offshore in February 1952. Note that the 10 TCs that spanned 2 different months were counted twice (once for each month).
        *   There are general increasing decadal trends in total TCs and TD but general decreasing decadal trends in TS, H, and MH. This could at least partially be explained by better observations of weaker systems over time. There also appears to be cycles of TCs, especially H, likely associated with the [Atlantic Multi-decadal Oscillation](https://www.noaa.gov/stories/atlantic-high-activity-eras-what-does-it-mean-for-hurricane-season).
        *   There is a general increasing trend of early (prior to June) and late (after October) season TCs, possibly related to improved observations over time.
        *   From 1950 to 2018, more TCs occurred during "cool" [El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)](https://www.climate.gov/enso) conditions (i.e.,La Nina) compared to "warm" ENSO conditions (i.e., El Nino). However, early in the season more TC occurred during El Nino conditions. Also, all 7 of the major (Cat 3+) hurricanes occurred during either La Nina or neutral ENSO conditions. Furthermore, there was a slight preference for more(and stronger) TCs during moderate-strong La Nina conditions compared to moderate-strong El Nino conditions.

*   [![Image 6: NWS Charleston, SC TC by Month/ENSO Phase (1950-2018)](https://www.weather.gov/images/chs/tropical/TCsByMonthENSOPhase.PNG)](https://www.weather.gov/images/chs/tropical/TCsByMonthENSOPhase.PNG "NWS Charleston, SC TC by Month/ENSO Phase (1950-2018)")

*   [![Image 8: NWS Charleston, SC TC Tracks During Moderate-Strong La Ninas (1950-2018) ](https://www.weather.gov/images/chs/tropical/ModStrong_LaNina_Tracks.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/chs/tropical/ModStrong_LaNina_Tracks.png "NWS Charleston, SC TC Tracks During Moderate-Strong La Ninas (1950-2018) ")
*   [![Image 9: NWS Charleston, SC TC Tracks During Moderate-Strong El Ninos (1950-2018) ](https://www.weather.gov/images/chs/tropical/ModStrong_ElNino_Tracks.png)](https://www.weather.gov/images/chs/tropical/ModStrong_ElNino_Tracks.png "NWS Charleston, SC TC Tracks During Moderate-Strong El Ninos (1950-2018) ")

*   _Landfalling TCs:_
    *   Since official records began in 1851 through 2018, 41 TCs made landfall in the [NWS Charleston, SC CWA](https://www.weather.gov/images/chs/misc/chs_cwa.jpg). 
        *   25 TCs were H, 9 were TS, and 7 were TD.
        *   17 TCs made landfall in Charleston County, SC, 9 in Beaufort County, SC,6 in Chatham County, GA, 4 in McIntosh County, GA, 3 in Liberty County, GA, and 2 in Colleton County, SC.
        *   Most landfalls occurred in August (12) and September (12), with the earliest landfalls (2) in May and the latest landfalls (7) in October.
        *   There has been a general upward trend in the number of weaker TCs making landfall (although this could at least partly be due to increasingly better observations over time) and a general downward trend in the number of major (Cat 3-5)hurricane landfalls.
        *   From 1950 to 2018, the most (9) landfalling TCs occurred during "neutral" [El Nino-Southern Oscillation (ENSO)](https://www.climate.gov/enso) conditions, including both major hurricanes(Gracie-1959 and Hugo-1989). In addition, roughly the same number of landfalls occurred during"warm" ENSO (i.e., El Nino) conditions (5) versus "cold" ENSO (i.e., La Nina) conditions (4), with a majority of these during "weak" El Nino/La Nina conditions.
        *   From 1950 to 2018, there was a slight preference for TCs to make landfall during the positive phase of the [North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO)](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/teleconnections/nao/)rather than during the negative phase.
        *   From 1950 to 2018, there was no preference for TCs to make landfall during either the positive or negative phases of the [Arctic Oscillation (AO)](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/teleconnections/ao/).

**Pre-1800**
1686 Sep 4-5"Spanish Repulse"Likely made landfall near Charleston causing extensive damage to ships, trees, crops, houses and livestock, and killed many people. After the storm, the Spanish aborted an invasion and turned back to FL.
1700 Sep 14"Rising Sun"Likely made landfall north of Charleston causing severe storm surge flooding despite winds shifting just before high tide, damage to several ships, including the 800-ton Scottish ship "Rising Sun", and 100+ deaths.
1713 Sep 16-17"Great Storm"Extremely destructive hurricane made landfall north of Charleston causing significant property damage and at least 70 deaths.
1722 Sep 19-21 Likely made landfall near Savannah causing significant flooding with the Savannah River over-spilling its banks.
1728 Aug 13-14 Likely made landfall just south of Charleston causing significant damage to ships, houses, wharfs, bridges and crops.
1752 Sep 13-15"Great Hurricane"Very strong (but likely small) hurricane made landfall just south of Charleston near high tide producing severe storm surge flooding (~17 ft MLW at Charleston), much property/crop/livestock damage and at least 95 deaths. It is likely the worst storm to ever hit Charleston. The storm occurred around the transition from the Julian to Gregorian calendars.
1783 Oct 6-8 Strong hurricane tracked along the coast causing significant property damage but not as much flooding as the 1752 storm.
**1800s**
1804 Sep 6-8 Large, violent (likely Cat 3 or 4) hurricane moved north near the GA coast before likely moving inland over southern SC. Produced significant wind/water damage around Charleston and killed hundreds of people.
1811 Sep 8-10 Hurricane likely made landfall south of Charleston causing a tornado which caused a lot of damage in the city.
1813 Aug 27 Brief but violent hurricane caused significant property damage and storm surge flooding similar to the 1752 storm and worse than the 1804 storm.
1822 Sep 27 Landfall just north of Charleston, SC as a small likely Cat 3 hurricane producing severe damage, mainly around the Santee River.
**Official Records Begin in 1851**

**_**Storms highlighted in red made landfall in the NWS Charleston County Warning Area (CWA)**_**
[1854](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1854.html)Sep 7-9"Great Carolina"Landfall just south of Savannah, GA as a large Cat 3 hurricane and then slowly tracked just east of Statesboro, GA as a Cat 1 hurricane before weakening to a TS as it crossed the Savannah River into Allendale County, SC. Although most of the significant wind damage was near/south of Charleston, SC, substantial storm surge flooding occurred well northward along the SC coast ruining many crops.
[1867](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1867.html)Jun 21-23 _*****Earliest landfalling hurricane in the NWS Charleston CWA*****_ Landfall at Isle of Palms, SC on June 22 as a Cat 1 hurricane and then weakened to a TS before moving through the Pee Dee and into central NC.
[1874](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1874.html)Sep 27-28 Landfall on Seabrook Island, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane. Produced downed telegraph lines and extensive wharf/crop damage in Charleston along with 2 deaths.
[1878](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1878.html)Sep 10-12 Landfall just south of Charleston, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane. Produced significant crop damage.
[1881](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1881.html)Aug 26-28 Landfall just south of Savannah, GA as a Cat 2 hurricane with winds ~105 mph before moving west into central GA and weakening into a TS. Produced significant surge flooding, property/crop damage and 700 U.S. deaths.
[1884](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1884.html)Sep 9-13 Landfall south of Savannah, GA on St. Catherine's Island as a TS. Weakened to a TD over land and re-curved out to sea off the SC coast before re-strengthening to a TS.
[1885](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1885.html)Aug 24-25 Landfall at Kiawah Island, SC as a Cat 2 hurricane causing significant damage along the GA/SC coasts northward through around Pawley's Island, SC and at least 21 deaths.
[1893](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1893.html)Aug 27-28"Great Sea Islands"_*****Earliest landfalling major hurricane in the NWS Charleston CWA*****_ Landfall just south of Savannah, GA on August 28 as a very large Cat 3 hurricane with peak winds near 115 mph and minimum pressure of 954 mb. Moved north-northeast through the SC Midlands and weakened to a Cat 1 hurricane before reaching Columbia, SC. The storm tide along the coast was catastrophic, a combination of the ~16 foot storm surge and the high astronomical tides. Significant wind/water damage occurred northward through around Charleston and [at least 1,000 (possibly 2,000+) people were killed](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/pdf/nws-nhc-6.pdf)in the U.S.. Fortunately, Savannah was spared complete inundation and less damage/deaths occurred in Charleston compared to the 1885 storm. However, the storm essentially marked the beginning of the end of rice cultivation and the phosphate industry in the region.
[1893](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1893.html)Oct 12-13 Moved northeast off the coasts of GA before making landfall along the SC coast just north of Charleston as a compact Cat 3 hurricane with 120 mph winds and minimum central pressure of 955 mb. Produced significant flooding due to already wet ground from previous storms.
[1894](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1894.html)Sep 26-27 Landfall on Hilton Head Island, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane before moving northeast and passing just west of Charleston with winds around 80 mph.
[1896](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1896.html)Sep 29 Tracked through southeast GA as a Cat 2/3 hurricane and through southeast SC as a Cat 1/2 hurricane. Produced significant wind damage around Savannah, GA and Beaufort, SC.
[1898](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1898.html)Aug 30-31 Landfall on Hilton Head Island, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane. Produced significant wind damage around Savannah and saltwater from the storm surge wrecked rice crops along the Savannah and Ogeechee Rivers.
[1898](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1898.html)Oct 1-3 Landfall on Cumberland Island, GA as a Cat 4 hurricane with winds near 130 mph. Moved northwest into central GA and weakened to a Cat 1 hurricane over Telfair County and then to a TS southwest of Macon. Produced a storm tide near 20 feet on Jekyll Island (with some significant flooding even around Savannah, GA), significant property damage across southeast GA and 179 U.S. deaths.
**1900s**
[1911](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1911.html)Aug 27-30 Landfall on Hilton Head Island, SC as a Cat 2 hurricane with winds near 100 mph. Moved slowly westward and weakened into a TS before reaching Statesboro, GA. Wind gusts reached 110 mph in Beaufort, SC, 96 mph in Savannah, GA, 95 mph on Edisto Island, SC and 94 mph at Charleston, SC (before the Weather Bureau's anemometer broke) causing many trees, power lines, and telegraph lines to fall. A significant storm surge produced extensive flood damage, especially from around Beaufort to Charleston. Much of the rice crops were destroyed, effectively ending the region's rice industry.
[1912](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1912.html)Jul 14-16 Landfall near Altamaha Sound, GA as a TS. Slowly moved west across southern GA producing heavy rain.
[1912](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1912.html)Sep 5-6 TS moved southwest off the SC coast before weakening into a TD and then making landfall on Ossabaw Island, GA.
[1913](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1913.html)Oct 7-10 Landfall on Cape Island, SC just north of Charleston as a Cat 1 hurricane. Produced heavy rain, especially in northeast SC, including 4"+ at Charleston.
[1916](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1916.html)May 15-16 _*****Earliest landfalling tropical storm in the NWS Charleston CWA*****_ Landfall on Fripp Island, SC as a TS on May 16.
[1916](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1916.html)Jul 13-15 Landfall at Bulls Bay, SC as a compact Cat 2 hurricane. The storm moved slowly and produced very heavy rain which caused severe river flooding. In fact, the Santee River at [Jamestown](https://water.noaa.gov/gauges/jams1) observed the highest water level on record. Damage was most significant north of Charleston and likely the worst in that area since the 1822 hurricane.
[1916](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1916.html)Oct 3-5 Landfall on Sapelo Island, GA as a TS.
[1927](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1927.html)Oct 2-3 Landfall near Edisto Beach, SC as a TS.
[1928](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1928.html)Sep 18"Lake Okeechobee"Landfall between Beaufort, SC and Charleston, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane. Produced some wind damage, mainly downed trees and power/phone lines, 1 1"+ of rain in Savannah, GA which caused significant flooding and ~$1 million in damage in Charleston.
[1940](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1940.html)Aug 10-13 Landfall near Hilton Head Island, SC as a Cat 2 hurricane with winds near 100 mph. Produced significant storm surge, 10+ inches of [rain](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/sehrcn1940.html)(mostly across SC).
[1945](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1945.html)Sep 16-17 Landfall near the GA/SC border as a TS. Produced gusts near 90 mph at Paris Island, SC, moderate flooding, and tornadoes with $6-7 million damage.
[1947](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1947.html)Oct 14-16 Landfall on Ossabaw Island, GA just south of Savannah as a Cat 2 hurricane with winds near 105 mph. Produced minor to moderate damage in Savannah as well as above normal tides in Charleston where minor flooding occurred. The lowest pressure at Savannah was 28.77 in Hg (974 mb), which is the 3rd lowest on record.
1950 Sep 6-7 Easy TD moved through southern GA. Produced [very heavy rainfall](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/easy1950.html), especially across coastal GA where 15+ inches fell (Savannah, GA recorded 16" inches).
[1952](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1952.html)Aug 30-31 Able Landfall near Beaufort, SC as a Cat 2 hurricane with sustained winds near 100 mph and minimum central pressure near 980 mb. Produced 90 mph winds at Beaufort, [heavy rainfall](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/able1952.html) over eastern SC and 2 deaths and $3 million in damage in SC.
[1953](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1953.html)Aug 31-Sep 1 TS approached the GA coast but weakened into a TD before making landfall south of Savannah, GA. The storm then moved inland through southeast GA and dissipated over central GA.
[1954](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1954.html)Oct 14-15[Hazel](https://www.weather.gov/ilm/HurricaneHazelAnniversary)Brushed the SC Lowcountry and made landfall near the SC/NC border as a Cat 4 hurricane with sustained winds near 130 mph, the strongest storm on record to make landfall that far north. Caused 95 deaths in the U.S. and was one of the worst storms on record in SC with significant damage, mainly from Pawleys Island northward.
[1959](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1959.html)Jul 4-9[Cindy](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/storm_wallets/atlantic/atl1959/cindy/)Landfall just north of Charleston, SC near Bulls Bay as a Cat 1 hurricane with winds near 75 mph winds. 64 mph winds were recorded at McClellanville along with 1 death. Storm tides were ~4 feet above normal and [heavy rain](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/cindy1959.html) fell.
[1959](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1959.html)Sep 28-30[Gracie](https://www.weather.gov/media/chs/events/HurricaneGracie1959.pdf)Landfall near Beaufort, SC as a Cat 4 hurricane with sustained winds near 130 mph and minimum pressure of 951 mb. Moved northwest past Columbia and weakened into a TS before moving into NC producing [heavy rainfall](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/gracie1959.html) which led to significant flooding as well as severe crop damage. Although a significant storm surge occurred (~9 feet at Charleston Harbor), the resulting flooding would have been much worse if the storm hit at high tide instead of low tide. The highest recorded storm tide was ~12 feet above mean low water (MLW) at Edisto Beach, SC. The relatively slow speed of the storm helped cause extensive wind/flooding damage across southeast SC, mainly in the Beaufort to Charleston corridor, along with 10 deaths in GA and SC. For more info, check out the [NHC archive](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/storm_wallets/atlantic/atl1959/gracie/).
[1960](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1960.html)Sep 11[Donna](https://www.hpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/donna1960.html)Landfall in the FL Keys as a Cat 4 hurricane and then moved northeast while weakening to a Cat 1 and then re-strengthening to a Cat 2 off the SC coast. Produced [heavy rain](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/donna1960.html), gusts near 70 mph on the coast near Charleston, tides ~2 feet above normal and a tornado that injured ~10 people and caused considerable damage in the Charleston area.
[1971](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1971.html)Sep 10-11 Landfall near Charleston, SC as a TD and then dissipated before moving west into GA.
[1976](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1976.html)Aug 19-21[Dottie](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/storm_wallets/atlantic/atl1976-prelim/dottie/)Landfall near Charleston, SC as a TS before dissipating north of Lake Moultrie.
[1979](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1979.html)Jun 15-16 TD approached the central SC coast from the south and made landfall near Kiawah Island before dissipating east of Columbia. Produced ~1-3 inches of [rainfall](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/td01aof1979.html) across the area.
[1979](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1979.html)Sep 4-5[David](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/storm_wallets/atlantic/atl1979-prelim/david/)Landfall on Sapelo Island, GA as a Cat 1 hurricane with winds ~90 mph. Produced 5 tornadoes, [heavy rainfall](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/david1979.html) (including 6.86" at Savannah), significant storm surge and beach erosion and ~$10 million in damage in SC. Savannah, GA recorded its 2nd lowest pressure on record (28.65" Hg / 970 mb).
[1981](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1981.html)Jul 3 TD moved north along the FL east coast and made landfall on Fripp Island, SC.
[1985](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1985.html)Jul 24-25[Bob](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/storm_wallets/atlantic/atl1985-prelim/bob/)Landfall on Fripp Island, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane. Produced a 44 mph wind gust in downtown Charleston, SC and a 48 mph gust at Folly Beach, SC. [5" of rain](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/bob1985.html)fell at the Charleston Airport.
[1988](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1988.html)Aug 28[Chris](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/storm_wallets/atlantic/atl1988-prelim/chris/)Landfall near Savannah, GA as a TS. Produced [heavy rainfall](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/chris1988.html) (~3 inches over eastern SC).
[1989](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1989.html)Sep 21-22[Hugo](https://www.weather.gov/chs/HurricaneHugo-Sep1989)Landfall at Sullivan's Island, SC as a Cat 4 hurricane with sustained winds near 140 mph producing very significant damage near Charleston. T he peak wind gust in Downtown Charleston was 108 mph, at Folly Beach it was 107 mph and in North Charleston at the airport it was 98 mph. Landfall occurred just before high tide but still resulted in peak storm tides of~20 feet above mean sea level at Romain Retreat, SC and 10-12 feet above mean sea level in Charleston Harbor. [Rainfall amounts](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/hugo1989.html)were limited due to the fast motion of the storm, although up to ~10 inches still occurred in southeast SC (highest total was 10.28 inches at Edisto Island). Check out our [25th anniversary video series in 2014](https://www.weather.gov/chs/Hugo25thAnniversary)about the storm and its impacts!
[1995](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1995.html)Aug 24-27[Jerry](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/AL111995_Jerry.pdf)Landfall near Palm Beach, FL as a TS and then slowly moved northwest toward the Big Bend area and weakened to a TD before moving north into east-central GA and eventually dissipating northwest of Augusta. Produced [heavy rainfall](https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/jerry1995.html), including a widespread area of 7+ inches over the Lowcountry/Coastal Empire and 10+ inches in some spots, including ~13 inches at Hilton Head Island, SC, ~11 inches at Savannah Airport, and ~7 inches at Charleston Airport.
[1999](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/1999.html)Sep 15[Floyd](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/AL081999_Floyd.pdf)Floyd was a large and intense Cape Verde storm that pounded parts of the Bahamas and threatened the entire Southeast U.S. coast. Floyd neared Cat 5 intensity in the Bahamas; however, it weakened thereafter and was a Cat 2 as it made landfall near Cape Fear, NC. Produced a 53 mph wind gust at the Savannah Airport and an 85 mph gust in Downtown Charleston. The minimum pressure at the Charleston Airport was 989.5 mb while [rainfall](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/floyd1999.html) totaled~4 inches at the Charleston Airport and in Downtown Charleston.
**2000s**
[2002](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2002.html)Oct 11-12[Kyle](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/AL122002_Kyle.pdf)Moved north-northeast along the GA/SC coasts before making landfall near McClellanville, SC as a TS. Produced [heavy rainfall](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/kyle2002.html) across coastal southeast GA and southeast SC (2.25 inches at the Savannah Airport and 4.91 inches at the Charleston Airport).
[2003](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2003.html)Jul 25-26#7 TD developed off the FL coast near Daytona Beach and moved northwest before making landfall at Sapelo Island, GA and then dissipating over central GA. Produced [heavy rainfall](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/td07aof2003.html), including ~5 inches near Savannah.
[2004](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2004.html)Aug 14[Charley](https://www.weather.gov/media/chs/events/PSHCHS_08162004.pdf)Landfall at Cape Romain, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane. Produced a peak wind gust of 38 mph and 1.02 inches of [rain](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/charley2004.html) at the Charleston Airport.
[2004](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2004.html)Aug 28-29[Gaston](https://www.weather.gov/chs/HurricaneGaston-Aug2004)Landfall near Awendaw, SC as a Cat 1 hurricane. Produced a peak wind gust of 55 mph and 4.05 inches of [rain](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/gaston2004.html) at the Charleston Airport and 4.63 inches in Downtown Charleston.
[2004](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2004.html)Sep 5-7 Frances Landfall on the FL coast near Stuart as a Cat 2 hurricane. The storm then moved into the northeast Gulf and made a second landfall along the Big Bend area of FL as a TS before moving into western GA and dissipating into a TD. [20 tornadoes](https://www.weather.gov/media/chs/events/PNSCHS_09202004.pdf) were documented across southeast SC and northern portions of southeast GA.
[2004](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2004.html)Sep 26-28[Jeanne](https://www.weather.gov/media/chs/events/PSHCHS_09302004.pdf)Landfall near Stuart, FL as a Cat 3 hurricane. The storm then moved up the west coast of FL and weakened into a TS before continuing into central GA and upstate SC as a TD. The storm produced ~1-3 inches of [rain](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/jeanne2004.html) and 6 confirmed weak tornadoes across southeast SC and northern portions of southeast GA.
[2005](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2005.html)Oct 5-6[Tammy](https://www.weather.gov/chs/TropicalStormTammy-Oct2005)Landfall near Atlantic Beach, FL as a TS. Moved northwest into southeast GA before weakening into a TD. Produced [very heavy rainfall](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/tammy2005.html) over southeast GA/SC, including localized amounts near 10 inches, especially over southeast GA where over 14 inches fell around Darien causing significant flooding.
[2006](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2006.html)Jun 13-14[Alberto](https://www.weather.gov/media/chs/events/PSHCHS_06152006.pdf)Landfall along the Big Bend area of FL as a TS. Moved northeast into southeast GA and weakened to a TD before moving into central SC and becoming an extra-tropical storm. Produced ~2-5 inches of [rain](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/alberto2006.html) across southeast SC/GA (3.29 inches of rain at the Savannah Airport and 2.51 inches at the Charleston Airport) with locally higher amounts ~7 inches (7.05 inches at Rincon, GA). In addition, 7 tornadoes were documented across southeast SC/GA in NWS Charleston's County Warning Area.
[2016](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2016.html)May 28-30[Bonnie](https://www.weather.gov/chs/TropicalStormBonnie-May2016)Developed north of the Bahamas and strengthened into a TS as it move northwest toward the GA/SC coasts, eventually weakening to a TD before making landfall near Charleston. Produced heavy rainfall (widespread 3-7 inches with local amounts over 10 inches), mainly north of I-16, which led to significant flooding.
[2016](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2016.html)Jun 6-7[Colin](https://www.weather.gov/chs/TropicalStormColin-June2016)Developed north of the Yucatan Peninsula and moved northeast while strengthening into a TS before making landfall around the Big Bend area of FL. Moved through southeast GA and then near the SC coast as a TS. Produced heavy rainfall (mainly 2-3 inches with locally higher amounts over 4 inches), which led to some flooding. Also produced some coastal flooding due to high storm tides.
[2016](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2016.html)Sep 1-3[Hermine](https://www.weather.gov/chs/TropicalStormHermine-Sep2016)Made landfall around the Big Bend area of FL as a Cat 1 hurricane and then moved northeast just inland through southeast GA and SC as a TS. Produced widespread tropical storm force wind gusts (60+ mph near the coast), heavy rainfall (widespread 3-5 inches with locally higher amounts over 8 inches toward the SC Midlands), and 2 EF-1 tornadoes (1 in Liberty County, GA and 1 in Chatham County, GA).
[2016](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2016.html)Sep 14-15[Julia](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2016/JULIA.shtml?)Developed near Jacksonville, FL as a TS and moved north and then northeast near the GA coast and then southern SC coast before moving east away from the coast and weakening to a TD. The storm then meandered well offshore while strengthening into a TS again and then weakening into a TD before dissipating.
[2016](http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2016.html)Oct 7-8[Matthew](https://www.weather.gov/chs/HurricaneMatthew-Oct2016)Moved north and then northwest through the Caribbean Sea and then through the Bahamas while strengthening to a Category 4 hurricane. Tracked just off the east coast of FL and GA while weakening to a Category 1 storm before making landfall near McClellanville, SC with winds near 85 mph. Produced hurricane force wind gusts along the entire coast, significant coastal flooding from high storm tides (including a record level at Fort Pulaski), and [very heavy rainfall](https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/matthew2016.html) (widespread 6 to 12 inches with locally higher amounts near 17 inches) which led to significant freshwater flooding.
[2017](https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/hurdat/2017.html)Sep 10-11[Irma](http://www.weather.gov/chs/TropicalStormIrma-Sep2017)M ade landfall in the FL Keys as a Cat 4 hurricane and then moved along the southwest coast of FL as a Category 3 hurricane. The storm then moved north near the west coast of FL while weakening to a TS before moving into southwest GA and continuing to weaken. Produced significant coastal flooding, [rainfall](https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/irma2017.html) flooding, and river flooding as well as near hurricane-force wind gusts and 4 tornadoes.
[2018](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2018&basin=atl)Sep 14-15[Florence](https://www.weather.gov/chs/TropicalStormFlorence-Sept2018)Made landfall near Wrightsville Beach, NC as a Cat 1 hurricane and then slowly shifted southwest into northeast SC as a TS. Produced TS force wind gusts and [heavy rain](http://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/florence2018.html) across the Charleston tri-county region but no significant impacts occurred.
[2019](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2019&basin=atl)Sep 4-5[Dorian](https://www.weather.gov/chs/HurricaneDorian-Sep2019)Cat 3 hurricane slowly moved north off the GA coast and then more northeast off the SC coast while weakening to a Cat 2 hurricane. Produced sustained TS force winds, hurricane force wind gusts, [heavy rain](https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/dorian2019.html)and some coastal flooding, especially along the SC coast.
[2020](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2020&basin=atl)May 27[Bertha](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/AL022020_Bertha.pdf)Developed just off the SC coast and made landfall near Isle of Palms, SC as a TS. Produced some [heavy rain](https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/bertha2020filledrainwhite.gif) and minor wind damage.
[2020](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2020&basin=atl)Aug 3[Isaias](https://www.weather.gov/chs/HurricaneIsaias-Aug2020)Tracked north-northeast just off the GA/SC coasts as a TS before strengthening to a Cat 1 hurricane ~50 miles east of Charleston, SC. Produced TS force wind gusts and[heavy rain](https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/isaias2020filledrainwhite.gif),mainly northeast of Charleston.
[2021](http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2021&basin=atl)Jun 28-29 Danny Landfall on Pritchards Island, SC as a very weak TS. Produced some [heavy rain](https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/danny2021filledrainwhite.gif) (~3-6") which caused some flooding.
[2021](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2021&basin=atl)Jul 7-8[Elsa](https://www.weather.gov/chs/TropicalStormElsa-July2021)Tracked northeast through southeast GA/central SC as a TS. Produced some significant impacts from hurricane force wind gusts and [heavy rain (8+ inches)](https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/elsa2021filledrainwhite.gif), mainly near the northern GA/southern SC coasts.
[2022](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2022&basin=atl)Sep 30[Ian](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/bd0750c3c312476ba9c8c59eb7cb3cce)On Friday, September 30, 2022 Hurricane Ian made landfall near Georgetown, SC as a Category 1 Hurricane. Ian [impacted the South Carolina Lowcountry](https://twitter.com/i/events/1580124737123983360) with strong gusty winds and torrential rainfall producing several flash flooding events.
[2022](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2022&basin=atl)Nov 10-11[Nicole](https://www.weather.gov/chs/TCNicole-2022)Nicole made landfall as a Category 1 Hurricane just south of Vero Beach, FL on Nov 10th. The system weakened to a tropical storm over inland FL, then weakened to a depression as it tracked over SW GA. The system produced [widespread rainfall across SE GA and SC](https://www.weather.gov/chs/TCNicole-2022), generally ranging between 1.5 to 3 inches.
[2023](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2023&basin=atl)Aug 30[Idalia](https://www.weather.gov/chs/Idalia2023)[Idalia](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/0a240641d793443ba8f808c942c354b4) moved from the northeastern Gulf region up through southeast GA and southeast SC before exiting back into the Atlantic just south of Myrtle Beach, SC. Tropical storm force winds were felt all along the southeast GA and southeast SC coastline. Very heavy rain fell across inland areas west of the Interstate-95 corridor leading to flooding in a number of locations. Idalia's passage coincident with high tide resulted in a damaging storm surge across portions of the SC coast.
[2024](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2024&basin=atl)Aug 4-9[Debby](https://www.weather.gov/chs/Debby2024)[Debby](https://www.weather.gov/chs/Debby2024) made landfall near the Big Bend of Florida as a hurricane on the morning of August 5th before weakening to a tropical storm and moving very slowly along the Southeast coast through August 9th. Prolonged heavy rainfall across southeast Georgia and southeast South Carolina brought widespread flash flooding on August 5th and 6th, with considerable and prolonged flooding of creeks, streams, and main stem rivers exacerbated by additional rainfall for several days thereafter. Additionally, several nighttime tornadoes occured across the South Carolina Low Country on the night of August 5th. Scattered tree damage from near-tropical-storm-force winds resulted in some power and communications outages.
[2024](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2024&basin=atl)Sep 15-26[#8](https://www.weather.gov/media/chs/TropicalEventSummary/PSHCHS_2024AL08_PTC8_Summary.pdf)This system began as an extra-tropical low center off the SC coast sometime on September 14. By the early morning of September 15, a Gale Warning was issued by the National Weather Service Office in Charleston, SC for the Charleston County nearshore Atlantic waters. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) designated this system as Potential Tropical Storm 8 (PTC8) by 5 pm on September 15, with a Tropical Storm Warning being issued for the Charleston County nearshore Atlantic waters, as well as Charleston and Berkeley Counties, in SC. Ultimately, this storm never became a tropical system as the elongated center moved slowly northwestward, reaching the Grand Strand coast of SC by late in the afternoon on September 16. Tropical storm force wind/wind gusts were confined to the marine waters and immediate coastal locations, which were occuring before the system was designated as PTC8. Tides were elevated for several days before and after the event. Tides reached high end moderate levels on the evening of September 15, while the center of storm circulation was eastsoutheast of the Charleston, SC area. There were also significant beach erosion reported along the Charleston County, SC coast.
[2024](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2024&basin=atl)Sep 24-27[Helene](https://www.weather.gov/chs/HurricaneHelene2024)[Hurricane Helene](https://www.weather.gov/chs/HurricaneHelene2024)made landfall as a Category 4 storm in the Florida Big Bend region west-southwest of Perry, Florida during the late evening of September 26. Helene then continued moving quickly northward into northeast Georgia by Friday morning, and across eastern Tennessee into central Kentucky by Friday evening, where it weakened to below tropical storm strength. The very large wind field associated with Helene produced widespread tropical storm force winds/wind gusts across most of southeast Georgia and southeast South Carolina during the evening and overnight hours of September 26-27. A few hurricane force wind gusts were also observed. The tropical storm force winds produced widespread tree damage and power outages with a few counties in southeast Georgia and southeast South Carolina reporting near 100 percent power outages. Additionally, conditions along the eastern side of the track of Helene were very conducive to tropical tornadoes, with numerous tornado warnings issued and several tornadoes confirmed across the region.
[2024](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2024&basin=atl)Oct 9-10 Milton Hurricane Milton rapidly deepened over the southwest Gulf, going from a tropical storm late in the night of October 5, to a Category Five hurricane by early in the afternoon of October 7 (about 27 hours!). Given the forecast from NHC was always for the storm to make landfall over the West-Central Florida coast, then move offshore of the East-Central Florida Coast, well south of our area into the Atlantic on October 10, our primary impact concerns were elevated tides and dangerous marine conditions. Despite days of northeast winds prior to the event, and then 12-24 hours of Tropical Storm Force winds over our Atlantic waters on October 10, the afternoon high tides on October 10 failed to even reach Coastal Flood Advisory levels. Tropical storm force wind/wind gusts were confined to the immediate coast, Atlantic waters and near the entrance of Charleston Harbor, with the highest winds beginning late night on October 9 over our southern area, and then advancing northward across the rest of our coast and Atlantic waters on October 10. Milton remained about 200 miles south of our area as it accelerated east-northward, away from the area, over the Atlantic. No significant rainfall was reported or expected. There were also no reports of any wind damage. It was suspected that there was at least minor to moderate beach erosion over our entire coastline, but no direct reports were received.
[2025](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?season=2025&basin=atl)Jul 4-6[Chantal](https://www.weather.gov/media/chs/TropicalEventSummary/PSHCHS_2025AL03_Chantal_Summary.pdf)A tropical disturbance off the Southeast coast developed into Tropical Depression 3 on July 4th, then strengthened to Tropical Storm Chantal on July 5th. Tropical Storm Chantal reached peak intensity, with winds up to 50 kt, late on the night of July 5th before making landfall near Litchfield Beach in Georgetown County early on the morning of July 6th. The strongest winds and heaviest rainfall occurred east of the center of the storm, sparing the Charleston area from any significant impacts.
